    Sensors — Readers#

    Instrument readers that decode L1 formats into calibrated, geolocated pyramids Datasets. For real MTG-FCI L1C FDHSI granules use read_fci_l1c: it decodes the packed radiance from the nested data/<channel>/measured groups, reads the per-granule calibration coefficients, and stitches the chunks by their geostationary geotransform Y origin (validated on real MTI1/Meteosat-12 granules — see issue #40). Read several channels in one call with channels=[...], which returns a dict[str, Dataset] and reads each chunk's structure and coefficients once for the whole set (e.g. the red/blue/near-IR bands of a true-colour composite); available_channels(chunks) lists which channels the chunk set carries (it also accepts a single chunk path). open_fci_l1c_chunk is the lower-level radiance opener for use with the generic read_fci (which also accepts channels=[...]).

    For MSG-SEVIRI Level-1.5 native (.nat) granules use read_seviri: it decodes a VIS/IR channel's 10-bit packed counts, applies the granule's per-channel Cal_Slope / Cal_Offset and the registry calibration, and returns the scene north-up on the 3 km geostationary grid (validated on a real Meteosat-10 granule — see issue #40). parse_seviri_native is the underlying .nat decoder, and a custom parse callable can still be injected.

    For Himawari-8/9 AHI Himawari Standard Data (.DAT) granules use read_ahi: it walks the 11 self-describing HSD header blocks, decodes the band's 16-bit counts, applies the granule's own count-to-radiance slope / intercept, masks the error (65535) and outside-scan (65534) sentinel counts, and returns the band north-up on its geostationary grid. Calibration prefers the coefficients the granule carries over the registry's nominal table: a solar band (1-6) uses the granule's c' as its band solar irradiance, and a thermal band (7-16) inverts Planck's law with the granule's own c / h / k and applies its quadratic Tb = c0 + c1*Te + c2*Te^2 correction — which the registry's linear alpha / beta form cannot express.

    A granule names its own band, so band is optional and merely asserts the expectation. A full disk ships as 10 segment files; pass the segment paths of one band together and they are stitched by their block #7 first-line numbers, with a gap or a duplicate reported rather than silently left blank. A contiguous subset is accepted too and returns only the lines it covers, georeferenced where they belong in the disk — so a partial download reads as the band of the disk it actually covers; completeness is not required, only contiguity. A single segment reads on its own the same way. .DAT.bz2 granules are decompressed transparently.

    The segments must come from one acquisition. Line numbers alone do not establish that, because every timeline numbers its segments identically — two scenes ten minutes apart would otherwise stitch into a seamless-looking image of two different moments. read_ahi therefore checks the satellite, the observation timeline and area, the declared segment count, and the projection block, and refuses a mixed set.

    Note it does not require the segments to share an observation start time. AHI scans the disk progressively, so each segment carries its own: on a real band-13 full disk, segments 1 and 10 start 526.0 s apart. The start times are only required to fall within an hour of each other, which separates the same timeline on different days without rejecting a legitimate scan.

    from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers import read_ahi

# one segment, calibrated to brightness temperature
bt = read_ahi("HS_H08_20150415_0230_B13_FLDK_R20_S0101.DAT")

# a stitched full disk from its 10 segments
import glob
disk = read_ahi(sorted(glob.glob("HS_H08_20150415_0230_B13_FLDK_R20_S*.DAT")))

    parse_ahi_hsd is the underlying decoder, returning uncalibrated radiance, and parse_hsd_header exposes the granule's grid, projection and calibration without reading its pixels.

    Because HSD carries no per-granule solar irradiance for the reflective bands in a form the registry can hold, ahi.yaml deliberately omits solar_irradiance: a solar calibration attempted without a granule raises CalibrationError rather than quietly using a value from elsewhere. See the table's own header for the provenance of every constant in it.

    One unit detail matters if you supply your own thermal coefficients or hand read_ahi a Dataset you built yourself. HSD is micrometre-based throughout: block #5 field 4 holds 10.4 for band 13 (not 1.04e-05), and the slope and intercept of the same block give radiance per micrometre, W / (m2 sr um). The registry's inverse Planck instead takes it per wavenumber, mW / (m2 sr (cm-1)-1). read_ahi rebases between the two itself — by L * wavelength_um**2 * 1e-1 — on every path that reaches the registry, so a Dataset source and an explicit coeffs= both calibrate correctly.

    The two bases differ by a factor of 1.5 (3.9 µm) to 17.7 (13.3 µm), which is the dangerous part: skipping the rebasing yields a plausible temperature rather than an obviously broken one — a 280 K scene reads as about 189 K. So a Dataset holding radiance in some other unit will not be rescued here, and the error will not announce itself: pass the granule, or convert before you call.

    (If you are reading the specification alongside this: every text extraction of the PDF loses its micro sign, so the wavelength and radiance units appear there as [m] and W / (m2 sr m). Table 1 listing the bands as 0.47 to 13.3 is what settles that they are micrometres.)

    Sentinel-3: swath readers#

    For Sentinel-3 .SEN3 granules use read_olci (OLCI L1B EFR / ERR) and read_slstr (SLSTR L1 RBT). Both decode through pyramids' bundled GDAL NetCDF driver — there is no netCDF4 dependency and nothing from the satpy stack — and available_olci_channels(granule) lists the OLCI bands a granule carries.

    These two differ from the geostationary readers above in three ways worth knowing:

    • They are swath instruments. A pushbroom sensor sweeps a curved strip of ground, so no affine geotransform can describe where the pixels are; the product instead ships a longitude and a latitude for every pixel. The results therefore carry a GDAL GEOLOCATION metadata domain pointing at those arrays, a placeholder pixel/line geotransform, and no CRS.

      Sentinel-3 stores those arrays CF-packed as int32 micro-degrees, and GDAL's geolocation transformer reads geolocation arrays raw, without applying scale_factor. The readers therefore point the domain at a small generated VRT that applies the packing, so the warp below receives real degrees rather than micro-degrees. The VRT is XML only — no geolocation array is read or copied until a warp pulls from it.

    Nothing is resampled — a caller who wants a map grid warps on demand:

    ```python
from osgeo import gdal
from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers import read_olci

swath = read_olci("S3A_OL_1_EFR.SEN3", channel="Oa08")
swath.geotransform          # the placeholder grid, not a geographic one
gdal.Warp("oa08.tif", swath.raster, geoloc=True)   # user-driven reprojection
```

    • They decode only. Radiometric calibration choices are out of scope for these readers (issue #136), so read_olci returns radiance and does not convert to reflectance; a caller converting it should use the granule's own per-detector solar_flux from instrument_data.nc. The SLSTR RBT product is already geophysical, so S7–S9 / F1–F2 arrive as brightness temperature in kelvin with no Planck conversion applied.

    • SLSTR is dual-view and multi-grid. It images each scene twice, so view="nadir" / "n" or "oblique" / "o" selects one. view defaults to None, which is not a synonym for nadir: a channel name may spell the view itself ("S8_BT_io"), and a spelled view wins — nadir is the fallback only when neither the channel nor view= names one. Its channels sit on different resolutions — S1–S6 on the 500 m a grid (with S4–S6 also on the alternative 500 m b), S7–S9 on the 1 km i grid, and of the fire channels F1 on f or i while F2 is i-only — they are asymmetric, and there is no F2_BT_f*.nc, so an f-less granule still reads F1 from i. grid= restricts a read to one grid and never falls back to another, so an explicit grid= can't quietly hand back a different resolution. available_slstr_channels(granule) reports what a granule carries on the grids of one view per call — view="nadir" unless you ask for "oblique" — which is how to discover a non-nominal layout. Because the grids differ in shape, channels=[...] returns a dict[str, Dataset] of differently-sized arrays rather than a stack.

    • OLCI comes as EFR or ERR. The two share every filename and variable name and differ only in pixel size (300 m against ~1200 m), so read_olci detects the product type from the granule name — falling back to xfdumanifest.xml — and reports resolution_m accordingly. A granule that identifies itself as neither carries no resolution_m at all, rather than a figure that could be wrong by a factor of four. (Nothing in this package reads that key today — harmonise takes an explicit reference grid — so it is provenance for a caller, not an input to the stack.)

    A reader keyword passed through read_file as a KEY=VALUE list arrives as a string, because Dataset.read_file normalises open_options to GDAL's form. The drivers therefore translate the string spellings of a boolean (false/true, yes/no, on/off, 1/0, case-insensitively) and reject a string they do not recognise, instead of treating the truthy "false" as switching the option on. A value that is not a string reaches the reader untouched, so the dict form with a real False is the unambiguous way to write it. Note that a channel set is a direct-call feature: read_file requires one Dataset back, so use read_olci(..., channels=[...]) when you want several at once.

    Himawari AHI (HSD) remains unimplemented: its byte-level layout comes from JMA's Himawari Standard Data User's Guide, which is needed before a correct decoder can be written (see issue #136).

    pyramids_eo.sensors.readers #

    Instrument readers — the package entry points.

    Each reader takes a file path / chunk set / Dataset and returns a pyramids Dataset / DatasetCollection (or curvilinear equivalent).

    • read_fci — MTG-FCI L1C (FDHSI): stitch a channel (or several — channels=[...] returns a dict) across its chunk set and calibrate to reflectance / brightness temperature.
    • read_fci_l1c — decode + stitch + calibrate one channel or several (channels=[...] returns a dict, opening each chunk once) across real MTG-FCI L1C FDHSI chunk files (packed radiance in nested groups, per-granule coefficients, geostationary grid).
    • available_channels — list the VIS/IR channels present in FCI L1C FDHSI chunk(s).
    • open_fci_l1c_chunk — lower-level open_chunk reading the FCI L1C FDHSI nested data/<channel>/measured/effective_radiance radiance for use with read_fci.
    • read_ahi — Himawari-8/9 AHI Himawari Standard Data (.DAT): decode one band from a granule (or stitch its segment set) and calibrate to reflectance / brightness temperature on the geostationary grid, using the granule's own coefficients.
    • parse_ahi_hsd — decode one HSD granule to a geolocated radiance Dataset (the uncalibrated layer under read_ahi).
    • parse_hsd_header / HsdHeader — decode the HSD header blocks from granule bytes the caller supplies, for the grid, projection and calibration without interpreting the pixels. It takes bytes rather than a path, so reading a granule's header alone means reading the file yourself; read_ahi does that internally when it sizes a stitch.
    • band_name / band_from_filename — AHI band keys (3 -> "B03"), and the band an HSD file name declares.
    • read_seviri — MSG-SEVIRI Level-1.5 native (.nat): decode + calibrate + geolocate a VIS/IR channel (via parse_seviri_native, or an injected parser).
    • parse_seviri_native — decode one VIS/IR channel of an MSG Level-1.5 native .nat granule to a geolocated radiance Dataset (the default read_seviri parser).
    • read_olci — Sentinel-3 OLCI L1B (EFR / ERR): decode one radiance band (or several — channels=[...] returns a dict) from a .SEN3 granule onto its native swath grid, geolocated by a GDAL GEOLOCATION domain.
    • available_olci_channels — list the OLCI radiance bands a .SEN3 granule carries.
    • product_type — tell an OLCI granule's EFR / ERR product apart (None when the granule names neither, or both), which is what fixes its ground resolution.
    • read_slstr — Sentinel-3 SLSTR L1 RBT: decode one channel (or several) for a chosen view (nadir / oblique) and grid, likewise swath-geolocated.
    • available_slstr_channels — list the channels, and grids per channel, an SLSTR granule can actually be read for in one view.
    • harmonise — align multi-resolution bands onto one common target grid.

    The Sentinel-3 readers decode to arrays plus CF metadata only — radiometric calibration choices stay with the caller (issue #136). Being swath instruments, their results carry a GDAL GEOLOCATION domain over the granule's per-pixel longitude / latitude arrays rather than an affine geotransform, and they resample nothing.

    HsdHeader dataclass #

    The HSD header fields a read needs, decoded from one granule.

    Attributes:

    Name Type Description
    satellite str

    Satellite name from block #1, as the granule spells it -- "Himawari-8" or "Himawari-9". This is a different vocabulary from the file name's H08 / H09 token, which :func:band_from_filename parses instead.
    band_number int

    AHI band number, 1-16 (block #5).
    columns int

    Pixels per line in this granule / segment (block #2).
    lines int

    Lines in this granule / segment (block #2).
    bits_per_pixel int

    Stored bit depth, always 16 for HSD (block #2).
    valid_bits int

    Valid bits per pixel for the band — 11, 12 or 14 depending on the band (block #5). Decoded and exposed, but deliberately not applied: the reader does not clip or mask counts that exceed 2**valid_bits. The two sentinel counts already identify every pixel the granule declares invalid, so a count above the valid range is a product defect rather than a flag, and silently discarding it would hide that defect instead of surfacing it. A caller that wants to treat the range as hard can read this field and mask.
    compression int

    Data-block compression flag — 0 none, 1 gzip, 2 bzip2.
    sub_lon float

    Sub-satellite longitude, degrees east (block #3).
    cfac int

    Column scaling factor of the normalised projection (block #3).
    lfac int

    Line scaling factor of the normalised projection (block #3).
    coff float

    Column offset — the sub-satellite column, 1-based (block #3).
    loff float

    Line offset — the sub-satellite line, 1-based (block #3).
    rs_km float

    Distance from the Earth's centre to the satellite (block #3).
    req_km float

    Ellipsoid equatorial radius, WGS84 (block #3).
    rpol_km float

    Ellipsoid polar radius, WGS84 (block #3).
    slope float

    Count-to-radiance slope actually in force (block #5); the calibrated (updated) value for a solar band when the granule carries one. Only its magnitude is screened — a negative gain decodes and is passed through (see :data:_MIN_SLOPE).
    intercept float

    Count-to-radiance intercept in force (block #5).
    error_count int

    Count value marking an error pixel (block #5, 65535).
    outside_count int

    Count value marking a pixel outside the scan area (block #5, 65534).
    central_wavelength_um float

    Band central wavelength in micrometres (block #5 field 4). HSD is micrometre-based throughout: the field carries 10.4 for band 13, not 1.04e-05, and the slope / intercept of the same block give radiance per micrometre. Every text extraction of the specification PDF loses its micro sign -- the whole document decodes to ASCII but for one multiplication sign -- so the unit renders as [m] there; Table 1 listing the bands as 0.47 to 13.3 is what settles it. The name carries the unit so the reading cannot drift again.
    albedo_coefficient float | None

    Solar bands only — c' of albedo = c' * radiance, so 1 / c' is the band solar irradiance; None for a thermal band.
    planck_c0 float | None

    Thermal bands only — constant term of the effective-to- brightness-temperature correction; None for a solar band.
    planck_c1 float | None

    Thermal bands only — linear term, else None.
    planck_c2 float | None

    Thermal bands only — quadratic term, else None.
    light_speed float | None

    Thermal bands only — speed of light the granule was calibrated with (m/s), else None.
    planck_constant float | None

    Thermal bands only — Planck constant (J s), else None.
    boltzmann_constant float | None

    Thermal bands only — Boltzmann constant (J/K), else None.
    total_segments int

    Number of segments the full image is split into (#7).
    segment_number int

    This granule's segment sequence number (block #7).
    first_line int

    1-based line of this segment within the full image (#7).
    observation_area str

    Observation-area token from block #1 ("FLDK" for a full disk), the same vocabulary as the file name's cccc field.
    observation_timeline int

    Observation timeline as hhmm (block #1).
    observation_start_mjd float

    Observation start time in Modified Julian Date (block #1). Per segment, not per image: AHI scans the disk progressively, so every segment of one acquisition carries its own. Measured on a real band-13 full disk, segments 1 and 10 start 526.0 s apart. It therefore does NOT identify an acquisition: observation_timeline with observation_area does so within one day -- that pair recurs daily -- and this field is only used to bound how far apart one acquisition's segments may start, which is what tells consecutive days apart (see :data:_MAX_ACQUISITION_SPAN_DAYS).
    total_header_length int

    Header length the granule declares (block #1), used to check the header walk rather than trusted blindly.
    total_data_length int

    Pixel-payload length the granule declares (block #1).

    Examples:

    • A decoded band-13 full-disk header reports its band, its radiometric kind, and the satellite height the projection is built from: 
      >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.ahi import HsdHeader
>>> header = HsdHeader(
...     satellite="Himawari-8", band_number=13, columns=5500, lines=5500,
...     bits_per_pixel=16, valid_bits=14, compression=0, sub_lon=140.7,
...     cfac=20466275, lfac=20466275, coff=2750.5, loff=2750.5,
...     rs_km=42164.0, req_km=6378.1370, rpol_km=6356.7523,
...     slope=0.5, intercept=-10.0, error_count=65535, outside_count=65534,
...     central_wavelength_um=10.4, albedo_coefficient=None,
...     planck_c0=0.0, planck_c1=1.0, planck_c2=0.0,
...     light_speed=299792458.0, planck_constant=6.62606957e-34,
...     boltzmann_constant=1.3806488e-23,
...     total_segments=10, segment_number=1, first_line=1,
...     observation_area="FLDK", observation_timeline=230,
...     observation_start_mjd=57127.1041666667,
...     total_header_length=1598, total_data_length=60500000,
... )
>>> header.band
'B13'
>>> header.kind
'thermal'
>>> round(header.satellite_height_m)
35785863

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
class HsdHeader:
    """The HSD header fields a read needs, decoded from one granule.

    Attributes:
        satellite: Satellite name from block #1, as the granule spells it --
            ``"Himawari-8"`` or ``"Himawari-9"``. This is a different vocabulary
            from the file name's ``H08`` / ``H09`` token, which
            :func:`band_from_filename` parses instead.
        band_number: AHI band number, 1-16 (block #5).
        columns: Pixels per line in this granule / segment (block #2).
        lines: Lines in this granule / segment (block #2).
        bits_per_pixel: Stored bit depth, always 16 for HSD (block #2).
        valid_bits: Valid bits per pixel for the band — 11, 12 or 14 depending on
            the band (block #5). Decoded and exposed, but deliberately **not**
            applied: the reader does not clip or mask counts that exceed
            ``2**valid_bits``. The two sentinel counts already identify every
            pixel the granule declares invalid, so a count above the valid range
            is a product defect rather than a flag, and silently discarding it
            would hide that defect instead of surfacing it. A caller that wants
            to treat the range as hard can read this field and mask.
        compression: Data-block compression flag — 0 none, 1 gzip, 2 bzip2.
        sub_lon: Sub-satellite longitude, degrees east (block #3).
        cfac: Column scaling factor of the normalised projection (block #3).
        lfac: Line scaling factor of the normalised projection (block #3).
        coff: Column offset — the sub-satellite column, 1-based (block #3).
        loff: Line offset — the sub-satellite line, 1-based (block #3).
        rs_km: Distance from the Earth's centre to the satellite (block #3).
        req_km: Ellipsoid equatorial radius, WGS84 (block #3).
        rpol_km: Ellipsoid polar radius, WGS84 (block #3).
        slope: Count-to-radiance slope actually in force (block #5); the
            calibrated (updated) value for a solar band when the granule
            carries one. Only its magnitude is screened — a negative gain
            decodes and is passed through (see :data:`_MIN_SLOPE`).
        intercept: Count-to-radiance intercept in force (block #5).
        error_count: Count value marking an error pixel (block #5, 65535).
        outside_count: Count value marking a pixel outside the scan area
            (block #5, 65534).
        central_wavelength_um: Band central wavelength in **micrometres**
            (block #5 field 4). HSD is micrometre-based throughout: the field
            carries 10.4 for band 13, not 1.04e-05, and the slope / intercept
            of the same block give radiance per micrometre. Every text
            extraction of the specification PDF loses its micro sign -- the
            whole document decodes to ASCII but for one multiplication sign --
            so the unit renders as ``[m]`` there; Table 1 listing the bands as
            0.47 to 13.3 is what settles it. The name carries the unit so the
            reading cannot drift again.
        albedo_coefficient: Solar bands only — ``c'`` of ``albedo = c' * radiance``,
            so ``1 / c'`` is the band solar irradiance; `None` for a thermal band.
        planck_c0: Thermal bands only — constant term of the effective-to-
            brightness-temperature correction; `None` for a solar band.
        planck_c1: Thermal bands only — linear term, else `None`.
        planck_c2: Thermal bands only — quadratic term, else `None`.
        light_speed: Thermal bands only — speed of light the granule was
            calibrated with (m/s), else `None`.
        planck_constant: Thermal bands only — Planck constant (J s), else `None`.
        boltzmann_constant: Thermal bands only — Boltzmann constant (J/K), else
            `None`.
        total_segments: Number of segments the full image is split into (#7).
        segment_number: This granule's segment sequence number (block #7).
        first_line: 1-based line of this segment within the full image (#7).
        observation_area: Observation-area token from block #1 (``"FLDK"`` for a
            full disk), the same vocabulary as the file name's ``cccc`` field.
        observation_timeline: Observation timeline as ``hhmm`` (block #1).
        observation_start_mjd: Observation start time in Modified Julian Date
            (block #1). **Per segment, not per image**: AHI scans the disk
            progressively, so every segment of one acquisition carries its own.
            Measured on a real band-13 full disk, segments 1 and 10 start 526.0 s
            apart. It therefore does NOT identify an acquisition:
            `observation_timeline` with `observation_area` does so **within one
            day** -- that pair recurs daily -- and this field is only used to
            bound how far apart one acquisition's segments may start, which is
            what tells consecutive days apart (see
            :data:`_MAX_ACQUISITION_SPAN_DAYS`).
        total_header_length: Header length the granule declares (block #1), used
            to check the header walk rather than trusted blindly.
        total_data_length: Pixel-payload length the granule declares (block #1).

    Examples:
        - A decoded band-13 full-disk header reports its band, its radiometric
          kind, and the satellite height the projection is built from:
            ```python
            >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.ahi import HsdHeader
            >>> header = HsdHeader(
            ...     satellite="Himawari-8", band_number=13, columns=5500, lines=5500,
            ...     bits_per_pixel=16, valid_bits=14, compression=0, sub_lon=140.7,
            ...     cfac=20466275, lfac=20466275, coff=2750.5, loff=2750.5,
            ...     rs_km=42164.0, req_km=6378.1370, rpol_km=6356.7523,
            ...     slope=0.5, intercept=-10.0, error_count=65535, outside_count=65534,
            ...     central_wavelength_um=10.4, albedo_coefficient=None,
            ...     planck_c0=0.0, planck_c1=1.0, planck_c2=0.0,
            ...     light_speed=299792458.0, planck_constant=6.62606957e-34,
            ...     boltzmann_constant=1.3806488e-23,
            ...     total_segments=10, segment_number=1, first_line=1,
            ...     observation_area="FLDK", observation_timeline=230,
            ...     observation_start_mjd=57127.1041666667,
            ...     total_header_length=1598, total_data_length=60500000,
            ... )
            >>> header.band
            'B13'
            >>> header.kind
            'thermal'
            >>> round(header.satellite_height_m)
            35785863

            ```

    @property
    def band(self) -> str:
        """Return the registry band key for this granule.

        Returns:
            The zero-padded ``"B<nn>"`` key for :attr:`band_number`, which is
            both the bundled registry's channel key and the band field of the
            HSD file name (e.g. ``"B13"``).
        """
        return band_name(self.band_number)

    @property
    def kind(self) -> str:
        """Return the band's radiometric kind.

        Returns:
            ``"solar"`` for bands 1-6 and ``"thermal"`` for bands 7-16 - the
            same split the specification uses to decide which variant of
            calibration block #5 a granule carries.

        Examples:
            - The split falls between bands 6 and 7, which is where the
              specification switches block #5 from its visible / near-infrared
              variant to its infrared one:
                ```python
                >>> import dataclasses
                >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.ahi import HsdHeader
                >>> header = HsdHeader(
                ...     satellite="Himawari-8", band_number=13, columns=5500, lines=5500,
                ...     bits_per_pixel=16, valid_bits=14, compression=0, sub_lon=140.7,
                ...     cfac=20466275, lfac=20466275, coff=2750.5, loff=2750.5,
                ...     rs_km=42164.0, req_km=6378.1370, rpol_km=6356.7523,
                ...     slope=0.5, intercept=-10.0, error_count=65535, outside_count=65534,
                ...     central_wavelength_um=10.4, albedo_coefficient=None,
                ...     planck_c0=0.0, planck_c1=1.0, planck_c2=0.0,
                ...     light_speed=299792458.0, planck_constant=6.62606957e-34,
                ...     boltzmann_constant=1.3806488e-23,
                ...     total_segments=10, segment_number=1, first_line=1,
                ...     observation_area="FLDK", observation_timeline=230,
                ...     observation_start_mjd=57127.1041666667,
                ...     total_header_length=1598, total_data_length=60500000,
                ... )
                >>> [dataclasses.replace(header, band_number=n).kind for n in (1, 6, 7, 16)]
                ['solar', 'solar', 'thermal', 'thermal']

                ```
        """
        return "solar" if self.band_number <= _SOLAR_BAND_MAX else "thermal"

    @property
    def satellite_height_m(self) -> float:
        """Return the satellite height above the ellipsoid, in metres.

        The projection block gives the distance from the Earth's *centre*; the
        geostationary CRS wants the perspective-point height above the equator,
        which is that distance less the equatorial radius.

        Returns:
            The perspective-point height in metres, derived from the granule's
            own ``Rs`` and ``req`` rather than from a hard-coded constant.
        """
        return (self.rs_km - self.req_km) * 1000.0

    def band_from_filename(path: Any) -> str | None:
    """Return the band key named by an HSD file name, when it follows Table 4.

    Args:
        path: Path to an HSD granule.

    Returns:
        The ``"B<nn>"`` band key the file name declares, or `None` when the name
        does not follow the HSD convention.

    Examples:
        - A conventional name yields its band; anything else yields `None`:
            ```python
            >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.ahi import band_from_filename
            >>> band_from_filename("HS_H08_20150415_0230_B13_FLDK_R20_S0101.DAT")
            'B13'
            >>> band_from_filename("scene.dat") is None
            True

            ```
    """
    match = _FILENAME_RE.match(str(path).replace("\\", "/").rsplit("/", 1)[-1])
    return None if match is None else band_name(int(match.group("band")))

    def parse_ahi_hsd(path: Any) -> Any:
    """Decode one HSD granule to a geolocated radiance `Dataset`.

    Reads the header, decodes the band's 16-bit counts, applies the granule's
    own count-to-radiance slope / intercept, masks the error and outside-scan
    sentinel counts to NaN, and registers the geostationary grid. A segment is
    georeferenced at its true place in the full image, so one segment reads on
    its own without being mistaken for the whole disk.

    Args:
        path: Path to a Himawari Standard Data ``.DAT`` (or ``.DAT.bz2``) granule.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` of spectral radiance on HSD's own
        per-micrometre-of-wavelength basis (``W m-2 sr-1 um-1``), on the
        geostationary grid, with the geostationary CRS and NaN nodata.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When the file is not a readable HSD granule (see
            :func:`parse_hsd_header` and :func:`_counts`).
    """
    buffer = _read_bytes(path)
    order = _byte_order(buffer)
    blocks = walk_header_blocks(buffer, order)
    header = _parse_header(buffer, order, blocks)
    radiance = _radiance(_counts(buffer, header, blocks, order), header)
    return _dataset(radiance, header, header.first_line)

    def parse_hsd_header(buffer: bytes) -> HsdHeader:
    """Decode the HSD header blocks a read depends on.

    Args:
        buffer: The granule bytes (already decompressed).

    Returns:
        The decoded :class:`HsdHeader`.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When the granule is not recognisable HSD, a block is
            truncated or mislabelled, block #1 contradicts the header walk, the
            band number is out of range, the grid is empty, a solar band's
            albedo coefficient is non-finite, or the count-to-radiance slope is
            unusable — non-finite, or of a magnitude below :data:`_MIN_SLOPE`.

    read_ahi(source, band=None, *, sensor='ahi', calibrate=True, sun_earth_distance=1.0, cos_sza=None, coeffs=None) #

    Read one AHI band from Himawari Standard Data into a Dataset.

    Decodes the band's counts to radiance with the granule's own calibration, then — when calibrate is set — converts to a physical quantity: reflectance for a solar band (1-6) and brightness temperature for a thermal one (7-16). Both conversions prefer the coefficients the granule carries over the registry's nominal table, so the result is granule-accurate.

    Pass the segment paths of one band together to read a stitched full disk; pass one path to read that segment alone, georeferenced where it belongs in the disk. A contiguous subset of the segments is also accepted and returns just those lines, so a partial download reads as the band of the disk it actually covers rather than being padded out or refused. The segments must come from one acquisition — same band, satellite, observation timeline and area — since line numbers alone repeat across timelines. Their observation start times differ, one per segment, because the disk is scanned progressively; the timeline and area are what identify the acquisition, and because that pair recurs daily the start times are bounded to within an hour of each other rather than compared for equality.

    def read_ahi(
    source: Any,
    band: Any = None,
    *,
    sensor: str = "ahi",
    calibrate: bool = True,
    sun_earth_distance: float = 1.0,
    cos_sza: Any = None,
    coeffs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> Any:
    """Read one AHI band from Himawari Standard Data into a `Dataset`.

    Decodes the band's counts to radiance with the granule's own calibration,
    then — when `calibrate` is set — converts to a physical quantity: reflectance
    for a solar band (1-6) and brightness temperature for a thermal one (7-16).
    Both conversions prefer the coefficients the granule carries over the
    registry's nominal table, so the result is granule-accurate.

    Pass the segment paths of one band together to read a stitched full disk;
    pass one path to read that segment alone, georeferenced where it belongs in
    the disk. A contiguous subset of the segments is also accepted and returns
    just those lines, so a partial download reads as the band of the disk it
    actually covers rather than being padded out or refused. The segments must
    come from one acquisition — same band, satellite, observation timeline and
    area — since line numbers alone repeat across timelines. Their observation
    *start times* differ, one per segment, because the disk is scanned
    progressively; the timeline and area are what identify the acquisition, and
    because that pair recurs daily the start times are bounded to within an hour
    of each other rather than compared for equality.

    Args:
        source: Path to an HSD ``.DAT`` / ``.DAT.bz2`` granule, an iterable of
            segment paths from one acquisition of one band, or a pyramids
            `Dataset` already holding the band radiance.
        band: The band to read (``13``, ``"B13"``, ``"band13"``). Optional: a
            granule names its own band, so this only has to be given to assert
            the expectation, and a mismatch is an error. Required when `source`
            is a `Dataset`, which carries no band metadata.
        sensor: Registry sensor name (default ``"ahi"``).
        calibrate: When `True` (default), calibrate to reflectance / brightness
            temperature; when `False`, return the raw radiance.
        sun_earth_distance: Sun-earth distance (AU) for solar-band reflectance.
            The default ``1.0`` leaves reflectance up to ~3.4% off (``d`` ranges
            ~0.983-1.017 AU over the year); pass the granule's ``d`` for absolute
            accuracy.
        cos_sza: Cosine of the solar zenith angle for the reflectance sun-angle
            correction, or `None`.
        coeffs: Per-granule calibration coefficients preferred over both the
            granule's own values and the registry (see
            :func:`~pyramids_eo.sensors.readers._common.calibrate_channel`), or
            `None`.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` of the calibrated (or raw) band. Read from a granule
        it carries the granule's own geostationary grid — the geostationary CRS,
        a metre geotransform and NaN nodata. Read from a `Dataset` source it
        keeps **that** dataset's geotransform, CRS and EPSG instead, since no HSD
        header is available to rebuild a grid from; only the values change.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When `source` is `None`, `band` is unknown or disagrees with
            the granule, a `Dataset` source is given without `band`, or the
            granule cannot be decoded.
        CalibrationError: When a band lacks the constants its kind needs.
        UnknownSensorError: When the sensor / band is not in the registry.
    """
    if source is None:
        raise ReaderError("read_ahi: source is required")
    requested = None if band is None else _canonical_band(band)

    if hasattr(source, "read_array"):
        if requested is None:
            raise ReaderError(
                "read_ahi: band is required when source is already a Dataset "
                "(it carries no HSD header to name the band)"
            )
        return _wrap_like(
            source,
            _calibrate_array(
                source.read_array(),
                requested,
                sensor=sensor,
                calibrate=calibrate,
                sun_earth_distance=sun_earth_distance,
                cos_sza=cos_sza,
                coeffs=coeffs,
                header=None,
            ),
        )

    paths = _resolve_paths(source)

    if len(paths) == 1:
        buffer = _read_bytes(paths[0])
        order = _byte_order(buffer)
        blocks = walk_header_blocks(buffer, order)
        header = _parse_header(buffer, order, blocks)
        # Checked against the header just parsed rather than with a second
        # header-only read, and before the pixels are touched either way.
        _assert_requested_band(header, requested)
        array = _radiance(_counts(buffer, header, blocks, order), header)
        first_line = header.first_line
    else:
        # `_stitch` parses every header before it decodes anything, so it makes
        # the same check there and no granule is read twice.
        array, header = _stitch(paths, requested=requested)
        first_line = header.first_line

    # Calibrate the values before registering them, so a full disk is wrapped
    # once rather than built as radiance and immediately rebuilt as brightness
    # temperature.
    return _dataset(
        _calibrate_array(
            array,
            header.band,
            sensor=sensor,
            calibrate=calibrate,
            sun_earth_distance=sun_earth_distance,
            cos_sza=cos_sza,
            coeffs=coeffs,
            header=header,
        ),
        header,
        first_line,
    )

    def open_fci_l1c_chunk(
    path: Any,
    channel: str,
    *,
    radiance_group: str = _FCI_RADIANCE_GROUP,
) -> Any:
    """Open one real FCI L1C FDHSI chunk from its nested group layout.

    Unlike `_default_open_chunk` (which assumes a flat variable named like the
    channel), this reads the radiance from the nested group path a real FCI L1C
    FDHSI chunk uses — by default `data/<channel>/measured/effective_radiance` —
    through pyramids' group-qualified `NetCDF.get_variable`, which navigates the
    `/`-separated group path. Pass it to `read_fci` as `open_chunk` for real
    granules:

    ```python
    from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers import open_fci_l1c_chunk, read_fci

    scene = read_fci(chunk_paths, "ir_105", open_chunk=open_fci_l1c_chunk)
    ```

    Warning:
        The nested group path matches the documented FDHSI layout, but has not
        been validated byte-for-byte against a real EUMETSAT granule, and this
        opener does not (yet) extract the per-granule calibration coefficients
        from the chunk's group attributes — supply them via
        `read_fci(..., coeffs=...)` or rely on the registry fallback. See issue
        #40.

    Args:
        path: Path to a single FCI L1C FDHSI chunk NetCDF file.
        channel: Channel identifier (e.g. `"ir_105"`), substituted into
            `radiance_group`.
        radiance_group: Group-qualified variable-name template with a single
            `{channel}` placeholder. Defaults to
            `data/{channel}/measured/effective_radiance`. `read_fci` calls the
            opener positionally, so to thread a non-default template through
            `read_fci` wrap it with
            `functools.partial(open_fci_l1c_chunk, radiance_group=...)`.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `NetCDF` variable view of the channel's raw effective radiance
        (a `Dataset`-like object exposing `read_array` / `geotransform` / `epsg` /
        `columns` / `rows`, as `read_fci` consumes it).
    """
    from pyramids.netcdf import NetCDF

    try:
        variable = radiance_group.format(channel=channel)
    except (KeyError, IndexError, ValueError, AttributeError, TypeError) as exc:
        raise ReaderError(
            f"invalid radiance_group template {radiance_group!r}: it must be a "
            f"format string with a single '{{channel}}' field ({exc!r})"
        ) from exc
    # Group navigation via get_variable needs the file opened as multidimensional;
    # pass it explicitly rather than relying on read_file's default.
    return NetCDF.read_file(str(path), open_as_multi_dimensional=True).get_variable(
        variable
    )

    def read_fci(
    chunks: Any,
    channel: str | None = None,
    *,
    channels: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    sensor: str = "fci",
    calibrate: bool = True,
    sun_earth_distance: float = 1.0,
    cos_sza: Any = None,
    coeffs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    open_chunk: Any = None,
) -> Any:
    """Read one or several FCI channels across a chunk set into `Dataset`s.

    For each requested channel, orders the chunks north -> south by their top-left
    latitude (so the caller may pass them in any order), stitches the radiance
    row-wise, calibrates it to reflectance (solar) or brightness temperature
    (thermal), and returns a geolocated pyramids `Dataset` carrying the
    northernmost chunk's CRS + geotransform. The chunks must share a CRS, cell
    size and column count and be vertically contiguous (validated per channel,
    since channels differ in resolution).

    Pass exactly one of `channel` (returns a `Dataset`) or `channels` (returns a
    `dict[str, Dataset]`); `read_fci(chunks, "ir_105")` is unchanged.

    Args:
        chunks: An ordered iterable of chunks, each either a pyramids `Dataset`
            already holding the channel radiance, or a value accepted by
            `open_chunk` (by default a NetCDF path).
        channel: A single channel identifier (e.g. `"ir_105"`, `"vis_06"`) for a
            `Dataset` result; mutually exclusive with `channels`.
        channels: A sequence of channel identifiers for a `dict[str, Dataset]`
            result; mutually exclusive with `channel`. (Each channel is opened via
            `open_chunk`, whose contract is per-channel; the grid is validated and
            ordered per channel because channels differ in resolution.)
        sensor: Registry sensor name (default `"fci"`).
        calibrate: When `True` (default), calibrate to a physical quantity; when
            `False`, return the stitched raw radiance.
        sun_earth_distance: Sun-earth distance (AU) for solar-channel reflectance.
        cos_sza: Cosine of the solar zenith angle for the reflectance sun-angle
            correction, or `None`.
        coeffs: Per-granule calibration coefficients preferred over the registry
            fallback (see `calibrate_channel`), or `None` to use the registry. They
            override a **single** channel's calibration, so they are only accepted
            with `channel=` — passing `coeffs` together with `channels=[...]` is an
            error (each channel would need its own).
        open_chunk: Callable `(chunk, channel) -> Dataset` used for chunks that
            are not already Datasets. Defaults to a NetCDF reader (see the module
            warning about the FCI layout).

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` (for `channel`) or a `dict[str, Dataset]` keyed by
        channel (for `channels`) of the calibrated (or raw) channel(s) on the
        stitched grid.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When neither / both of `channel` / `channels` are given, or
            when `chunks` is empty.
        CalibrationError: When a channel lacks the constants its kind needs.
        UnknownSensorError: When the sensor / channel is not in the registry.
    """
    requested, single = resolve_channels(channel, channels, "read_fci")
    chunk_list = list(chunks)
    if not chunk_list:
        raise ReaderError("read_fci: no chunks given")
    # A pre-opened Dataset holds exactly one channel's radiance, so it cannot serve
    # a multi-channel request — every channel would alias the same array. Reject it
    # rather than return a physically meaningless dict.
    if not single and any(hasattr(chunk, "read_array") for chunk in chunk_list):
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_fci: channels=[...] needs path-like chunks read per channel via "
            "open_chunk; a pre-opened Dataset already holds a single channel"
        )
    # `coeffs` overrides one channel's calibration; sharing it across a channel set
    # would mis-calibrate the others. Require the single-channel form for an override.
    if not single and coeffs is not None:
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_fci: `coeffs` overrides a single channel's calibration; pass it "
            "with `channel=`, not `channels=[...]` (each channel calibrates on its own)"
        )
    opener = open_chunk or _default_open_chunk

    from pyramids.base.crs import crs_spec
    from pyramids.dataset import Dataset, GeoReference

    results = {}
    for name in requested:
        datasets = [
            chunk if hasattr(chunk, "read_array") else opener(chunk, name)
            for chunk in chunk_list
        ]
        _validate_chunk_grid(datasets)
        # Order the chunks north -> south by their top-left latitude/y so the
        # stitch and geolocation are correct regardless of the order the chunks
        # were passed in (FCI files are commonly numbered south -> north).
        ordered = sorted(datasets, key=lambda ds: ds.geotransform[3], reverse=True)
        radiance = np.concatenate(
            [np.asarray(ds.read_array(), dtype=float) for ds in ordered], axis=0
        )
        data = (
            calibrate_channel(
                radiance, name, sensor, sun_earth_distance, cos_sza, coeffs=coeffs
            )
            if calibrate
            else radiance
        )
        north = ordered[0]
        # Calibration can produce NaN (terminator reflectance / non-positive
        # radiance), so declare NaN as nodata rather than the default -9999.
        results[name] = Dataset.from_array(
            data,
            geo_ref=GeoReference(
                geo=north.geotransform, epsg=crs_spec(north.epsg, north.crs)
            ),
            no_data_value=np.nan,
        )
    return results[requested[0]] if single else results

    def available_channels(chunks: Any) -> list[str]:
    """List the VIS/IR channels present across FCI L1C FDHSI chunk file(s).

    Opens each chunk's multidimensional dataset and reports the `data/<channel>`
    groups that carry an `effective_radiance` array, so a caller can discover the
    channel names instead of hard-coding them. The union across chunks is returned
    (a trailer chunk contributes none), sorted.

    Args:
        chunks: A single chunk path, or an iterable of chunk paths. (For
            convenience this discovery helper also accepts a lone path, whereas
            `read_fci_l1c` / `read_fci` take an iterable of chunk paths.)

    Returns:
        The sorted channel identifiers available in the chunk(s).
    """
    paths = [chunks] if isinstance(chunks, (str, bytes, os.PathLike)) else list(chunks)
    found: set[str] = set()
    for path in paths:
        found |= _channels_in_chunk(path)
    return sorted(found)

    def read_fci_l1c(
    paths: Any,
    channel: str | None = None,
    *,
    channels: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    calibrate: bool = True,
    sun_earth_distance: float = 1.0,
    cos_sza: Any = None,
) -> Any:
    """Read one or several channels across a set of real FCI L1C FDHSI chunks.

    Decodes each chunk once for the whole requested channel set
    (`read_fci_l1c_chunks` opens the chunk's structure a single time), drops chunks
    without a channel's radiance (e.g. `CHK-TRAIL`), then for each channel orders
    the chunks north -> south by their geotransform Y origin, checks they are
    vertically contiguous (and share a grid), stitches the radiance, and calibrates
    it with the **per-granule** coefficients (reflectance for a solar channel,
    brightness temperature for a thermal one). Each result is a geolocated pyramids
    `Dataset` on the granule's geostationary grid (metre geotransform reconstructed
    from the angular grid and the CRS satellite height, with its x axis reconciled
    to the CRS so a warp is not mirrored east-west — issue #56).

    Pass exactly one of `channel` (returns a `Dataset`) or `channels` (returns a
    `dict[str, Dataset]`); `read_fci_l1c(paths, "ir_105")` is unchanged.

    Args:
        paths: Iterable of FCI L1C FDHSI chunk file paths (any order; trailer /
            non-imagery chunks are skipped).
        channel: A single channel identifier (e.g. `"ir_105"`, `"vis_06"`) for a
            `Dataset` result; mutually exclusive with `channels`.
        channels: A sequence of channel identifiers for a `dict[str, Dataset]`
            result (each chunk opened once for the whole set); mutually exclusive
            with `channel`.
        calibrate: When `True` (default), calibrate to reflectance / brightness
            temperature; when `False`, return the stitched raw radiance.
        sun_earth_distance: Sun-earth distance (AU) for solar-channel reflectance.
            The default `1.0` leaves reflectance up to ~3.4% off (`d` ranges
            ~0.983-1.017 AU over the year); pass the granule's `d` for absolute
            accuracy.
        cos_sza: Cosine of the solar zenith angle for the reflectance sun-angle
            correction, or `None`.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` (for `channel`) or a `dict[str, Dataset]` keyed by
        channel (for `channels`) of the calibrated (or raw) channel(s) on the
        stitched geostationary grid, with NaN nodata and the geostationary CRS.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When neither / both of `channel` / `channels` are given, when
            no chunk carries a requested channel, or the chunks are inconsistent
            (mixed CRS / cell size / column count, or not vertically contiguous —
            see `_validate_chunks`).
        CalibrationError: When a channel lacks the constants its kind needs.
        UnknownSensorError: When a channel is not in the registry.
    """
    requested, single = resolve_channels(channel, channels, "read_fci_l1c")

    per_channel: dict[str, list] = {name: [] for name in requested}
    for path in paths:
        for name, record in read_fci_l1c_chunks(path, requested).items():
            if record is not None:
                per_channel[name].append(record)

    results = {
        name: _assemble_channel(
            per_channel[name],
            name,
            calibrate=calibrate,
            sun_earth_distance=sun_earth_distance,
            cos_sza=cos_sza,
        )
        for name in requested
    }
    return results[requested[0]] if single else results

    def available_olci_channels(source: Any) -> list[str]:
    """List the OLCI radiance bands a granule actually carries.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or a file inside it.

    Returns:
        The canonical channel names present, sorted (`["Oa01", "Oa02", ...]`).

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When `source` is not a granule directory or a file in one.
    """
    granule = resolve_granule(source, "available_olci_channels")
    found = []
    for number in range(1, _BAND_COUNT + 1):
        channel = f"Oa{number:02d}"
        if (granule / _band_filename(channel)).is_file():
            found.append(channel)
    return found

    product_type(granule) #

    Detect whether a granule is the full- or reduced-resolution OLCI product.

    EFR and ERR granules hold the same OaNN_radiance.nc filenames and the same variable names, so the product type -- and therefore the ground resolution, 300 m against ~1200 m -- is only knowable from the granule's own naming or its manifest. Both are checked -- the name first, then xfdumanifest.xml -- and None means neither identified the product, in which case the reader reports no resolution rather than asserting a wrong one.

    An ambiguous source is treated exactly like a silent one: a text carrying both tokens yields None rather than the first match, because an ERR granule routinely references the EFR product it was derived from, so preferring either one would be a guess (see _product_tokens).

    def product_type(granule: Path) -> str | None:
    """Detect whether a granule is the full- or reduced-resolution OLCI product.

    EFR and ERR granules hold the **same** `OaNN_radiance.nc` filenames and the
    same variable names, so the product type -- and therefore the ground
    resolution, 300 m against ~1200 m -- is only knowable from the granule's own
    naming or its manifest. Both are checked -- the name first, then
    `xfdumanifest.xml` -- and `None` means neither identified the product, in
    which case the reader reports no resolution rather than asserting a wrong one.

    An **ambiguous** source is treated exactly like a silent one: a text carrying
    both tokens yields `None` rather than the first match, because an ERR granule
    routinely references the EFR product it was derived from, so preferring either
    one would be a guess (see `_product_tokens`).

    Args:
        granule: The `.SEN3` granule directory.

    Returns:
        `"EFR"`, `"ERR"`, or `None` -- when the granule does not identify itself,
        and equally when it names both products.

    Examples:
        - A standard product name identifies itself, so no file access is needed:
            ```python
            >>> from pathlib import Path
            >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
            >>> product_type(Path("S3A_OL_1_EFR____20230101T101530.SEN3"))
            'EFR'
            >>> product_type(Path("S3B_OL_1_ERR____20230101T101530.SEN3"))
            'ERR'

            ```
        - A granule that names neither, and carries no manifest saying so, yields
          `None` -- which is what makes the reader omit `resolution_m` rather than
          guess it:
            ```python
            >>> from pathlib import Path
            >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
            >>> product_type(Path("mystery.SEN3")) is None
            True

            ```
        - A name claiming both products is ambiguous, so it too yields `None`
          rather than the first token found:
            ```python
            >>> from pathlib import Path
            >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
            >>> product_type(Path("S3A_OL_1_ERR____from_OL_1_EFR_source.SEN3")) is None
            True

            ```
    """
    found = _product_tokens(granule.name.upper(), "_OL_1_")
    if found is not None:
        return found
    manifest = granule / "xfdumanifest.xml"
    if manifest.is_file():
        try:
            text = manifest.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").upper()
        except OSError:
            return None
        return _product_tokens(text, "OL_1_")
    return None

    read_olci(source, channel=None, *, channels=None, geolocation=True) #

    Read one or several OLCI L1B radiance bands from a .SEN3 granule.

    Decodes each requested band's packed OaNN_radiance variable (raw * scale_factor + add_offset, with the _FillValue and anything outside the variable's validity limits masked to NaN) and returns it as a swath Dataset carrying the granule's per-pixel geolocation as a GDAL GEOLOCATION domain. The limits come from the valid_min / valid_max scalars the OLCI L1 specification carries -- not from a combined valid_range, which appears nowhere in it -- and are compared against the raw, still-packed values.

    Pass exactly one of channel (returns a Dataset) or channels (returns a dict[str, Dataset] keyed by canonical channel name).

    This reader decodes only -- it does not convert radiance to reflectance (issue #136 scopes radiometric calibration choices out). The granule's instrument_data.nc carries the per-detector solar_flux a caller needs for that conversion.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    source Any

    The .SEN3 granule directory, or any file inside it.

    		 required
    channel str | None

    A single band ("Oa08"); mutually exclusive with channels.

    		 None
    channels Sequence[str] | None

    A sequence of bands for a dict result; mutually exclusive with channel.

    		 None
    geolocation bool

    When True (default), attach each result's per-pixel GEOLOCATION domain from geo_coordinates.nc.

    		 True

    Returns:

    Type Description
    Any

    A pyramids Dataset (for channel) or a dict[str, Dataset] (for
    Any

    channels), each on the granule's native swath grid with NaN nodata.

    Raises:

    Type Description
    ReaderError

    When neither / both of channel / channels are given, channels is empty or has duplicates, a band name is not an OLCI band, or the granule lacks a requested band. A channel set whose bands come back on different shapes also raises: the one geolocation domain is shared across the set, which is only sound because the bands of a granule share a grid, so a granule that breaks that is reported rather than geolocated against the wrong grid. With geolocation=True, also when geo_coordinates.nc or its variables are missing, its grid's shape differs from the bands', or it carries an unusable scale_factor / add_offset.
    Note

    A _FillValue that is not a finite number cannot mask anything, so the decode emits a UserWarning per affected band and the result's nodata is incomplete rather than the read failing (see invalid_mask).

    def read_olci(
    source: Any,
    channel: str | None = None,
    *,
    channels: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    geolocation: bool = True,
) -> Any:
    """Read one or several OLCI L1B radiance bands from a `.SEN3` granule.

    Decodes each requested band's packed `OaNN_radiance` variable (`raw *
    scale_factor + add_offset`, with the `_FillValue` and anything outside the
    variable's validity limits masked to NaN) and returns it as a swath `Dataset`
    carrying the granule's per-pixel geolocation as a GDAL `GEOLOCATION` domain.
    The limits come from the `valid_min` / `valid_max` scalars the OLCI L1
    specification carries -- not from a combined `valid_range`, which appears
    nowhere in it -- and are compared against the raw, still-packed values.

    Pass exactly one of `channel` (returns a `Dataset`) or `channels` (returns a
    `dict[str, Dataset]` keyed by canonical channel name).

    This reader **decodes only** -- it does not convert radiance to reflectance
    (issue #136 scopes radiometric calibration choices out). The granule's
    `instrument_data.nc` carries the per-detector `solar_flux` a caller needs for
    that conversion.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or any file inside it.
        channel: A single band (`"Oa08"`); mutually exclusive with `channels`.
        channels: A sequence of bands for a `dict` result; mutually exclusive
            with `channel`.
        geolocation: When `True` (default), attach each result's per-pixel
            `GEOLOCATION` domain from `geo_coordinates.nc`.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` (for `channel`) or a `dict[str, Dataset]` (for
        `channels`), each on the granule's native swath grid with NaN nodata.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When neither / both of `channel` / `channels` are given,
            `channels` is empty or has duplicates, a band name is not an OLCI
            band, or the granule lacks a requested band. A channel set whose bands
            come back on **different** shapes also raises: the one geolocation
            domain is shared across the set, which is only sound because the bands
            of a granule share a grid, so a granule that breaks that is reported
            rather than geolocated against the wrong grid. With
            `geolocation=True`, also when `geo_coordinates.nc` or its variables are
            missing, its grid's shape differs from the bands', or it carries an
            unusable `scale_factor` / `add_offset`.

    Note:
        A `_FillValue` that is not a finite number cannot mask anything, so the
        decode emits a `UserWarning` per affected band and the result's nodata is
        incomplete rather than the read failing (see `invalid_mask`).
    """
    requested, single = resolve_channels(channel, channels, "read_olci")
    # Canonicalise before the duplicate check: `resolve_channels` compares the raw
    # strings, so aliases of one band ("Oa08" and "oa8") slip through it and would
    # otherwise collapse into a single dict entry, silently dropping a requested band.
    canonical = [_canonical_channel(name, "read_olci") for name in requested]
    if len(set(canonical)) != len(canonical):
        duplicates = sorted({c for c in canonical if canonical.count(c) > 1})
        raise ReaderError(
            f"read_olci: `channels` names the same band more than once (after "
            f"normalising spellings): {duplicates}"
        )
    # Resolve the granule and its geolocation domain ONCE for the whole set,
    # matching read_fci_l1c's documented read-each-chunk-once pattern rather than
    # re-running them per channel.
    reader = "read_olci"
    granule = resolve_granule(source, reader)
    # Detect the product type once for the whole set rather than per band: it may
    # read xfdumanifest.xml, which a 21-band read would otherwise re-parse 21 times.
    product = product_type(granule)
    decoded = {name: _read_band(granule, name, reader) for name in canonical}
    shapes = {name: values.shape for name, (values, _) in decoded.items()}
    if len(set(shapes.values())) > 1:
        raise ReaderError(
            f"read_olci: the requested bands are not on one grid: {shapes}; OLCI "
            f"bands of a granule share a grid, so this granule looks inconsistent"
        )
    first = next(iter(decoded.values()))[0]
    domain = _resolve_domain(granule, reader, first.shape) if geolocation else {}
    results = {
        name: _wrap_band(granule, name, values, variable_meta, domain, product)
        for name, (values, variable_meta) in decoded.items()
    }
    return results[canonical[0]] if single else results

    def parse_seviri_native(
    path: Any, channel: str, *, subsatellite_longitude: float = 0.0
) -> Any:
    """Decode one VIS/IR channel of an MSG Level-1.5 native (`.nat`) granule.

    Reads the segment table and the fixed-layout ``15Header`` (reference grid,
    grid step and the per-granule calibration), then unpacks the channel's 10-bit
    counts from every image line record, applies the granule ``Cal_Slope`` /
    ``Cal_Offset`` to get radiance, masks the zero-count (off-earth) corners to
    NaN, and orients the scene north-up / west-left. Only the image lines
    actually present are read, so a header-preserved subset (whose header still
    declares the full disk) decodes correctly rather than reading past end-of-file.

    Args:
        path: Path to an MSG SEVIRI Level-1.5 native `.nat` file.
        channel: A VIS/IR channel identifier (e.g. `"IR_108"`, `"VIS006"`); HRV
            is not supported.
        subsatellite_longitude: Sub-satellite longitude (degrees east) for the
            geostationary CRS. Defaults to `0.0`, the nominal prime service
            (`MSG15`); pass the service longitude for IODC (41.5) or rapid-scan
            (9.5) granules, whose `.nat` header the reader does not parse for it.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` holding the channel radiance on the geostationary
        grid, with the geostationary CRS, a metre geotransform, and NaN nodata.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When the channel is unknown / HRV, the file is not a
            recognised MSG Level-1.5 native granule (no segment table, or the
            ``15Header`` layout / calibration fails its sanity checks), the file
            carries no complete line record, or the decoded line records are not
            contiguous (an unexpected channel selection or layout).
    """
    if channel == "HRV":
        raise ReaderError("read_seviri: HRV is not supported (different geometry)")
    try:
        position = _VISIR_CHANNELS.index(channel)
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise ReaderError(
            f"read_seviri: unknown SEVIRI VIS/IR channel {channel!r}"
        ) from exc

    try:
        handle = open(path, "rb")
    except OSError as exc:
        raise ReaderError(f"read_seviri: cannot open {path} ({exc})") from exc
    with handle:
        segments = _segments(handle.read(_PRODUCT_HEADER_SCAN_BYTES))
        try:
            header_length, header_offset = segments["15Header"]
            data_length, data_offset = segments["15Data"]
        except KeyError as exc:
            raise ReaderError(
                "read_seviri: no 15Header/15Data segment table "
                f"(not an MSG Level-1.5 native file?) — {path}"
            ) from exc
        handle.seek(header_offset)
        header = handle.read(header_length)
        if len(header) < _CALIBRATION_OFFSET + 12 * 16:
            raise ReaderError(
                "read_seviri: 15Header is truncated "
                "(not a supported MSG Level-1.5 native file)"
            )
        file_size = os.fstat(handle.fileno()).st_size

    lines_declared, columns = struct.unpack_from(">ii", header, _REF_GRID_OFFSET)
    line_step_km, column_step_km = struct.unpack_from(">ff", header, _GRID_STEP_OFFSET)
    # The reference grid and grid step sit immediately before the calibration
    # block: sane values here confirm the fixed 15Header layout was found. The
    # line and column steps must match (the VIS/IR grid is isotropic 3 km).
    if not (
        lines_declared == columns
        and 1000 <= columns <= 12000
        and 2.9 < column_step_km < 3.1
        and np.isclose(line_step_km, column_step_km)
        and columns % 4 == 0
    ):
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_seviri: unexpected 15Header layout (reference grid / grid step "
            "sanity check failed) — not a supported MSG Level-1.5 native file"
        )
    pixel_m = column_step_km * 1000.0

    slope, offset = struct.unpack_from(
        ">dd", header, _CALIBRATION_OFFSET + position * 16
    )
    if slope <= 0:
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_seviri: non-physical calibration slope (unexpected header layout)"
        )

    if data_length % lines_declared:
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_seviri: 15Data length is not a whole number of line records"
        )
    stride = data_length // lines_declared
    packed_bytes = columns * 10 // 8
    # The 11 VIS/IR channels precede HRV in every record; assume the standard
    # all-channel product so channel `position` maps straight to block `position`.
    # The contiguity check below rejects a file where that assumption does not hold.
    block_start = position * (_LINE_SIDE_INFO_BYTES + packed_bytes)
    data_start = block_start + _LINE_SIDE_INFO_BYTES
    if data_start + packed_bytes > stride:
        raise ReaderError("read_seviri: channel block exceeds the line-record stride")

    # The declared 15Data holds exactly `lines_declared` records; a full product
    # has a 15Trailer segment after it, so cap the count at the declared line
    # count. Without this cap the trailer bytes get read as extra "line records",
    # break the +1 contiguity of `line_numbers`, and reject a valid full disk.
    # The file-size term still handles a header-preserved subset (fewer records).
    available = min((file_size - data_offset) // stride, lines_declared)
    if available < 1:
        raise ReaderError("read_seviri: file carries no complete image line record")

    counts = np.empty((available, columns), dtype=np.uint16)
    line_numbers = np.empty(available, dtype=np.int64)
    with (
        open(path, "rb") as handle,
        mmap.mmap(handle.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ) as mapped,
    ):
        for index in range(available):
            record = data_offset + index * stride
            line_numbers[index] = struct.unpack_from(
                ">i", mapped, record + block_start + _LINE_NUMBER_OFFSET
            )[0]
            start = record + data_start
            counts[index] = _unpack_10bit(mapped[start : start + packed_bytes], columns)

    if not np.all(np.diff(line_numbers) == 1):
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_seviri: image line records are not contiguous "
            "(unexpected channel selection or record layout)"
        )

    radiance = counts.astype(float) * slope + offset
    radiance[counts == 0] = np.nan  # zero counts mark the off-earth space corners
    # The grid origin is South-East: line numbers increase northward and the
    # stored columns run east -> west (the first column is East). Reverse both
    # axes for a north-up, west-left raster. Copy the flipped view to a
    # C-contiguous array so no downstream consumer trips on the negative strides.
    radiance = np.ascontiguousarray(radiance[::-1, ::-1])

    # CGMS/EUMETSAT navigation places the sub-satellite point at the CENTRE of the
    # reference pixel N/2 (0-based, both axes; e.g. pixel 1856 of the 3712 grid) —
    # the COFF = LOFF convention, which reproduces the published MSG full-disk area
    # extent (west edge -(N/2 + 0.5) * px). All columns are present (full width) so
    # the SSP column is N/2; only a subset of lines may be present, so the SSP row
    # is N/2 measured from the northmost present line (row 0 after the north-up
    # flip). Register the metre geotransform so that reference pixel's centre is
    # (x=0, y=0).
    reference = columns / 2.0  # == lines_declared / 2.0 for the square VIS/IR grid
    ssp_row = int(line_numbers[-1]) - reference
    x_west_edge = -(reference + 0.5) * pixel_m
    y_north_edge = (ssp_row + 0.5) * pixel_m
    geo = (x_west_edge, pixel_m, 0.0, y_north_edge, 0.0, -pixel_m)

    from pyramids.dataset import Dataset, GeoReference

    dataset = Dataset.from_array(
        radiance, geo_ref=GeoReference(geo=geo, epsg=None), no_data_value=np.nan
    )
    dataset.crs = _geostationary_wkt(subsatellite_longitude)
    return dataset

    read_seviri(source, channel, *, sensor='seviri', calibrate=True, sun_earth_distance=1.0, cos_sza=None, coeffs=None, parse=None, subsatellite_longitude=0.0) #

    coeffs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    parse: Any = None,
    subsatellite_longitude: float = 0.0,
) -> Any:
    """Read one SEVIRI channel into a calibrated, geolocated `Dataset`.

    Decodes the channel radiance (from a `.nat` granule via `parse`, or straight
    from a `Dataset` source), then calibrates it to reflectance (solar) or
    brightness temperature (thermal) via the registry and returns a pyramids
    `Dataset` carrying the source's CRS + geotransform.

    Args:
        source: A path to an MSG Level-1.5 native `.nat` file (decoded by
            `parse`), or a pyramids `Dataset` already holding the channel radiance.
        channel: Channel identifier (e.g. `"IR_108"`, `"VIS006"`).
        sensor: Registry sensor name (default `"seviri"`).
        calibrate: When `True` (default), calibrate to a physical quantity; when
            `False`, return the raw radiance.
        sun_earth_distance: Sun-earth distance (AU) for solar-channel reflectance.
            The default `1.0` leaves reflectance up to ~3.4% off (`d` ranges
            ~0.983-1.017 AU over the year); pass the granule's `d` for absolute
            accuracy.
        cos_sza: Cosine of the solar zenith angle for the reflectance sun-angle
            correction, or `None`.
        coeffs: Per-granule calibration coefficients preferred over the registry
            fallback (see `calibrate_channel`), or `None` to use the registry.
        parse: Callable `(source, channel) -> Dataset` used when `source` is not
            already a `Dataset`. Defaults to the native `.nat` parser
            (`parse_seviri_native`).
        subsatellite_longitude: Sub-satellite longitude (degrees east) passed to
            the default native parser for the geostationary CRS (default `0.0`,
            the prime service); ignored when a custom `parse` is supplied.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` of the calibrated (or raw) channel.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When `source` is `None`, or the native parse fails.
        CalibrationError: When a channel lacks the constants its kind needs.
        UnknownSensorError: When the sensor / channel is not in the registry.
    """
    if source is None:
        raise ReaderError("read_seviri: source is required")

    if hasattr(source, "read_array"):
        dataset = source
    elif parse is not None:
        dataset = parse(source, channel)
    else:
        dataset = parse_seviri_native(
            source, channel, subsatellite_longitude=subsatellite_longitude
        )
    radiance = np.asarray(dataset.read_array(), dtype=float)
    data = (
        calibrate_channel(
            radiance, channel, sensor, sun_earth_distance, cos_sza, coeffs=coeffs
        )
        if calibrate
        else radiance
    )

    from pyramids.dataset import Dataset, GeoReference

    # Calibration can produce NaN (terminator reflectance / non-positive
    # radiance), so declare NaN as nodata rather than the default -9999.
    epsg = dataset.epsg if dataset.epsg else None
    result = Dataset.from_array(
        data,
        geo_ref=GeoReference(geo=dataset.geotransform, epsg=epsg),
        no_data_value=np.nan,
    )
    if epsg is None:
        # A non-EPSG CRS (e.g. the geostationary grid) must be carried explicitly.
        result.crs = dataset.crs
    return result

    def available_slstr_channels(
    source: Any, *, view: str = "nadir"
) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    """Report which channels a granule carries in one view, and on which grids.

    This is how a caller discovers a product's real layout rather than assuming
    it -- including that `F2` lives on the 1 km `i` grid while `F1` is on `f`, and
    which of `S4`-`S6` are duplicated onto the alternative 500 m `b` grid.

    A grid is listed only when the granule holds **both** the measurement file and
    the `geodetic_<grid><view>.nc` the measurement needs, so what this reports is
    what `read_slstr` can actually return -- a measurement whose annotation file is
    missing would raise there, and listing it would promise a read that fails. A
    granule stripped of its geodetic files therefore reports `{}` even though the
    measurement files are all present.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or a file inside it.
        view: `"nadir"` (default) or `"oblique"`.

    Returns:
        A `{channel: [grid letters]}` mapping listing only the channels the granule
        holds a measurement **and** a matching geodetic file for, in the product's
        own channel order -- `S1`..`S9` then `F1`, `F2` -- which is not the
        alphabetical order the error messages use. Each channel's grid letters are
        likewise in the order `read_slstr` would try them.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When `source` is not a granule, or `view` is not an SLSTR
            view.
    """
    reader = "available_slstr_channels"
    suffix = _resolve_view(view, reader)
    granule = resolve_granule(source, reader)
    found: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
    for channel, (grids, quantity) in _CHANNEL_GRIDS.items():
        present = [
            letter
            for letter in grids
            if (granule / f"{channel}_{quantity}_{letter}{suffix}.nc").is_file()
            and (granule / f"geodetic_{letter}{suffix}.nc").is_file()
        ]
        if present:
            found[channel] = present
    return found

    read_slstr(source, channel=None, *, channels=None, view=None, grid=None, geolocation=True) #

    Read one or several SLSTR L1 RBT channels from a .SEN3 granule.

    Decodes each requested channel's packed variable (raw * scale_factor + add_offset, with the _FillValue and anything outside the variable's validity limits masked to NaN) and returns it as a swath Dataset carrying the matching grid's per-pixel geolocation as a GDAL GEOLOCATION domain. The limits come from the valid_min / valid_max scalars the SLSTR L1 specification carries -- not from a combined valid_range, which appears nowhere in it -- and are compared against the raw, still-packed values.

    Pass exactly one of channel (returns a Dataset) or channels (returns a dict[str, Dataset]). Channels on different grids have different array shapes, which is why a channel set returns a dict rather than a stack.

    Either may also be given in the product's own variable spelling ("S5_radiance_bn"), and the grid and view it carries then select the file: they are honoured, not merely tolerated. So a channel set may mix views and grids per channel -- channels=["S5_radiance_an", "S8_BT_io"] reads one nadir and one oblique -- while view= / grid= supply whatever a bare spelling leaves open. A spelling that contradicts an explicit view= / grid= is an error rather than one of the two being silently ignored.

    This reader decodes only -- issue #136 scopes radiometric calibration choices out. The RBT product is already geophysical, so S7-S9 / F1-F2 arrive as brightness temperature in kelvin with no conversion applied.
