    def read_slstr(
    source: Any,
    channel: str | None = None,
    *,
    channels: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    view: str | None = None,
    grid: str | None = None,
    geolocation: bool = True,
) -> Any:
    """Read one or several SLSTR L1 RBT channels from a `.SEN3` granule.

    Decodes each requested channel's packed variable (`raw * scale_factor +
    add_offset`, with the `_FillValue` and anything outside the variable's
    validity limits masked to NaN) and returns it as a swath `Dataset` carrying
    the matching grid's per-pixel geolocation as a GDAL `GEOLOCATION` domain. The
    limits come from the `valid_min` / `valid_max` scalars the SLSTR L1
    specification carries -- not from a combined `valid_range`, which appears
    nowhere in it -- and are compared against the raw, still-packed values.

    Pass exactly one of `channel` (returns a `Dataset`) or `channels` (returns a
    `dict[str, Dataset]`). Channels on different grids have **different array
    shapes**, which is why a channel set returns a dict rather than a stack.

    Either may also be given in the product's own variable spelling
    (`"S5_radiance_bn"`), and the grid and view it carries then **select the
    file**: they are honoured, not merely tolerated. So a channel set may mix views
    and grids per channel -- `channels=["S5_radiance_an", "S8_BT_io"]` reads one
    nadir and one oblique -- while `view=` / `grid=` supply whatever a bare
    spelling leaves open. A spelling that contradicts an explicit `view=` / `grid=`
    is an error rather than one of the two being silently ignored.

    This reader **decodes only** -- issue #136 scopes radiometric calibration
    choices out. The RBT product is already geophysical, so `S7`-`S9` / `F1`-`F2`
    arrive as brightness temperature in kelvin with no conversion applied.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or any file inside it.
        channel: A single channel (`"S5"`, or `"S5_radiance_bn"`); mutually
            exclusive with `channels`.
        channels: A sequence of channels for a `dict` result; mutually exclusive
            with `channel`. The dict is keyed by **canonical** channel name, so two
            spellings of one channel -- even on different grids, as
            `["S5_radiance_an", "S5_radiance_bn"]` -- are rejected as a duplicate
            rather than collapsing into one entry.
        view: `"nadir"` or `"oblique"` -- SLSTR images each scene twice. `None`
            (default) takes each channel's view from its own spelling, falling back
            to nadir for a bare one.
        grid: An explicit grid letter (`"a"`, `"b"`, `"i"`, `"f"`) restricting
            every channel to that one grid. `None` (default) uses a spelled grid
            where one is given and otherwise tries the channel's documented grids
            in order. A restricted read never falls back to another resolution: a
            channel the granule does not carry on that grid raises instead.
        geolocation: When `True` (default), attach each result's `GEOLOCATION`
            domain.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` (for `channel`) or a `dict[str, Dataset]` (for
        `channels`), each on its native swath grid with NaN nodata.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When neither / both of `channel` / `channels` are given,
            `channels` is empty or names a channel twice, a channel or the view
            is not an SLSTR one, a spelled channel names a quantity that channel
            does not ship or a grid / view contradicting an explicit `grid=` /
            `view=`, `grid` is not one of the four SLSTR grid letters, or the
            granule lacks a requested channel on the grid(s) tried. With
            `geolocation=True`, also when a channel's geodetic annotation is
            missing, is on a grid whose shape differs from the band, or carries an
            unusable `scale_factor` / `add_offset`.

    Note:
        A `_FillValue` that is not a finite number cannot mask anything, so the
        decode emits a `UserWarning` per affected channel and the result's nodata
        is incomplete rather than the read failing (see `invalid_mask`).
    """
    requested, single = resolve_channels(channel, channels, "read_slstr")
    # Canonicalise before the duplicate check: `resolve_channels` compares the raw
    # strings, so aliases of one channel ("S5" and "s5") slip through it and would
    # otherwise collapse into a single dict entry, silently dropping a request.
    canonical = [_canonical_channel(name, "read_slstr") for name in requested]
    if len(set(canonical)) != len(canonical):
        duplicates = sorted({c for c in canonical if canonical.count(c) > 1})
        raise ReaderError(
            f"read_slstr: `channels` names the same channel more than once (after "
            f"normalising spellings): {duplicates}"
        )
    # Pass the caller's ORIGINAL spelling through, not the canonical name: a
    # spelled grid and view select a specific file, and canonicalising first would
    # strip them and read a different one.
    # Resolve the granule once for the whole set rather than per channel, matching
    # read_fci_l1c's and read_olci's read-once pattern.
    granule = resolve_granule(source, "read_slstr")
    results = {
        name: read_slstr_band(
            granule, spelling, view=view, grid=grid, geolocation=geolocation
        )
        for name, spelling in zip(canonical, requested)
    }
    return results[canonical[0]] if single else results

    pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.fci_l1c #

    Real MTG-FCI L1C FDHSI granule reader.

    read_fci_l1c decodes and stitches one channel — or several in a single pass (channels=[...] returns a dict, reading each chunk's structure and coefficients once for the whole set) — across the real FCI L1C FDHSI chunk files of a repeat cycle, and available_channels lists which channels a chunk carries. Unlike the generic read_fci (which stitches already-opened radiance Datasets), this reads the actual granule layout:

    • the packed uint16 radiance from the nested group data/<channel>/measured/effective_radiance, unpacked to physical radiance via the variable's scale_factor / add_offset and masked by its valid_range / _FillValue;
    • the per-granule calibration coefficients carried as sibling variables in the same group (radiance_to_bt_conversion_coefficient_a / _b / _wavenumber for thermal channels, channel_effective_solar_irradiance for solar ones), preferred over the nominal registry table;
    • the chunks are ordered and stitched by their geostationary geotransform Y origin (FCI's start_position_row runs opposite to the geospatial Y, so it is read as metadata but is not the stitch key); a chunk that carries no radiance for the channel — e.g. the CHK-TRAIL trailer — is skipped.

    The granule stores the grid in geostationary angular (radian) coordinates with a metre geostationary CRS; the metre geotransform is reconstructed as angular_geotransform * satellite_height (from the CRS +h). This addresses the axis-unit mismatch behind pyramids #706 by keeping the CRS explicit rather than letting it be misread as lon/lat. FCI's x is a scanning azimuth angle whose sign runs opposite to PROJ's geostationary x (which increases eastward), so the scaled x pixel width comes out negative with its origin on the eastern limb; the reader reconciles it to the CRS — re-anchoring the origin on the western limb with a positive x width, the array left untouched — so a warped scene is not mirrored east-west (issue #56).

    Validated against real MTI1/Meteosat-12 FDHSI chunks (see issue #40): ir_105 stitches to brightness temperature in the expected range on the geostationary grid. The reader uses GDAL (already vendored by pyramids) to read the nested groups and scalar variables — no extra dependency.

    def read_fci_l1c(
    paths: Any,
    channel: str | None = None,
    *,
    channels: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    calibrate: bool = True,
    sun_earth_distance: float = 1.0,
    cos_sza: Any = None,
) -> Any:
    """Read one or several channels across a set of real FCI L1C FDHSI chunks.

    Decodes each chunk once for the whole requested channel set
    (`read_fci_l1c_chunks` opens the chunk's structure a single time), drops chunks
    without a channel's radiance (e.g. `CHK-TRAIL`), then for each channel orders
    the chunks north -> south by their geotransform Y origin, checks they are
    vertically contiguous (and share a grid), stitches the radiance, and calibrates
    it with the **per-granule** coefficients (reflectance for a solar channel,
    brightness temperature for a thermal one). Each result is a geolocated pyramids
    `Dataset` on the granule's geostationary grid (metre geotransform reconstructed
    from the angular grid and the CRS satellite height, with its x axis reconciled
    to the CRS so a warp is not mirrored east-west — issue #56).

    Pass exactly one of `channel` (returns a `Dataset`) or `channels` (returns a
    `dict[str, Dataset]`); `read_fci_l1c(paths, "ir_105")` is unchanged.

    Args:
        paths: Iterable of FCI L1C FDHSI chunk file paths (any order; trailer /
            non-imagery chunks are skipped).
        channel: A single channel identifier (e.g. `"ir_105"`, `"vis_06"`) for a
            `Dataset` result; mutually exclusive with `channels`.
        channels: A sequence of channel identifiers for a `dict[str, Dataset]`
            result (each chunk opened once for the whole set); mutually exclusive
            with `channel`.
        calibrate: When `True` (default), calibrate to reflectance / brightness
            temperature; when `False`, return the stitched raw radiance.
        sun_earth_distance: Sun-earth distance (AU) for solar-channel reflectance.
            The default `1.0` leaves reflectance up to ~3.4% off (`d` ranges
            ~0.983-1.017 AU over the year); pass the granule's `d` for absolute
            accuracy.
        cos_sza: Cosine of the solar zenith angle for the reflectance sun-angle
            correction, or `None`.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` (for `channel`) or a `dict[str, Dataset]` keyed by
        channel (for `channels`) of the calibrated (or raw) channel(s) on the
        stitched geostationary grid, with NaN nodata and the geostationary CRS.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When neither / both of `channel` / `channels` are given, when
            no chunk carries a requested channel, or the chunks are inconsistent
            (mixed CRS / cell size / column count, or not vertically contiguous —
            see `_validate_chunks`).
        CalibrationError: When a channel lacks the constants its kind needs.
        UnknownSensorError: When a channel is not in the registry.
    """
    requested, single = resolve_channels(channel, channels, "read_fci_l1c")

    per_channel: dict[str, list] = {name: [] for name in requested}
    for path in paths:
        for name, record in read_fci_l1c_chunks(path, requested).items():
            if record is not None:
                per_channel[name].append(record)

    results = {
        name: _assemble_channel(
            per_channel[name],
            name,
            calibrate=calibrate,
            sun_earth_distance=sun_earth_distance,
            cos_sza=cos_sza,
        )
        for name in requested
    }
    return results[requested[0]] if single else results

    def available_channels(chunks: Any) -> list[str]:
    """List the VIS/IR channels present across FCI L1C FDHSI chunk file(s).

    Opens each chunk's multidimensional dataset and reports the `data/<channel>`
    groups that carry an `effective_radiance` array, so a caller can discover the
    channel names instead of hard-coding them. The union across chunks is returned
    (a trailer chunk contributes none), sorted.

    Args:
        chunks: A single chunk path, or an iterable of chunk paths. (For
            convenience this discovery helper also accepts a lone path, whereas
            `read_fci_l1c` / `read_fci` take an iterable of chunk paths.)

    Returns:
        The sorted channel identifiers available in the chunk(s).
    """
    paths = [chunks] if isinstance(chunks, (str, bytes, os.PathLike)) else list(chunks)
    found: set[str] = set()
    for path in paths:
        found |= _channels_in_chunk(path)
    return sorted(found)

    pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.fci #

    MTG-FCI L1C (FDHSI) reader.

    read_fci stitches a channel across the ~40 NetCDF chunks of one FCI repeat cycle, calibrates the raw radiance to reflectance / brightness temperature via the sensor registry, and returns a geolocated pyramids Dataset ready for to_crs / warped_view.

    Warning

    The zero-config default (_default_open_chunk) assumes each chunk exposes the requested channel's radiance as a NetCDF variable named like the channel. Real FCI L1C FDHSI stores radiance in nested groups (data/<channel>/measured/effective_radiance) with the calibration coefficients in group attributes — for those granules pass open_fci_l1c_chunk (which reads that nested layout) as open_chunk, plus the coefficients via coeffs. The stitch + calibrate + geolocate logic is unit-tested on synthetic chunks, and open_fci_l1c_chunk is unit-tested for its group-path resolution, but the exact FCI variable layout and the per-granule coefficient attributes still need validation against a real granule (see issue #40).

    open_fci_l1c_chunk(path, channel, *, radiance_group=_FCI_RADIANCE_GROUP) #

    Open one real FCI L1C FDHSI chunk from its nested group layout.

Pass it to read_fci as open_chunk for real granules:

    def open_fci_l1c_chunk(
    path: Any,
    channel: str,
    *,
    radiance_group: str = _FCI_RADIANCE_GROUP,
) -> Any:
    """Open one real FCI L1C FDHSI chunk from its nested group layout.

    Unlike `_default_open_chunk` (which assumes a flat variable named like the
    channel), this reads the radiance from the nested group path a real FCI L1C
    FDHSI chunk uses — by default `data/<channel>/measured/effective_radiance` —
    through pyramids' group-qualified `NetCDF.get_variable`, which navigates the
    `/`-separated group path. Pass it to `read_fci` as `open_chunk` for real
    granules:

    ```python
    from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers import open_fci_l1c_chunk, read_fci

    scene = read_fci(chunk_paths, "ir_105", open_chunk=open_fci_l1c_chunk)
    ```

    Warning:
        The nested group path matches the documented FDHSI layout, but has not
        been validated byte-for-byte against a real EUMETSAT granule, and this
        opener does not (yet) extract the per-granule calibration coefficients
        from the chunk's group attributes — supply them via
        `read_fci(..., coeffs=...)` or rely on the registry fallback. See issue
        #40.

    Args:
        path: Path to a single FCI L1C FDHSI chunk NetCDF file.
        channel: Channel identifier (e.g. `"ir_105"`), substituted into
            `radiance_group`.
        radiance_group: Group-qualified variable-name template with a single
            `{channel}` placeholder. Defaults to
            `data/{channel}/measured/effective_radiance`. `read_fci` calls the
            opener positionally, so to thread a non-default template through
            `read_fci` wrap it with
            `functools.partial(open_fci_l1c_chunk, radiance_group=...)`.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `NetCDF` variable view of the channel's raw effective radiance
        (a `Dataset`-like object exposing `read_array` / `geotransform` / `epsg` /
        `columns` / `rows`, as `read_fci` consumes it).
    """
    from pyramids.netcdf import NetCDF

    try:
        variable = radiance_group.format(channel=channel)
    except (KeyError, IndexError, ValueError, AttributeError, TypeError) as exc:
        raise ReaderError(
            f"invalid radiance_group template {radiance_group!r}: it must be a "
            f"format string with a single '{{channel}}' field ({exc!r})"
        ) from exc
    # Group navigation via get_variable needs the file opened as multidimensional;
    # pass it explicitly rather than relying on read_file's default.
    return NetCDF.read_file(str(path), open_as_multi_dimensional=True).get_variable(
        variable
    )

    read_fci(chunks, channel=None, *, channels=None, sensor='fci', calibrate=True, sun_earth_distance=1.0, cos_sza=None, coeffs=None, open_chunk=None) #

The chunks must share a CRS, cell size and column count and be vertically contiguous (validated per channel, since channels differ in resolution).

    def read_fci(
    chunks: Any,
    channel: str | None = None,
    *,
    channels: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    sensor: str = "fci",
    calibrate: bool = True,
    sun_earth_distance: float = 1.0,
    cos_sza: Any = None,
    coeffs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    open_chunk: Any = None,
) -> Any:
    """Read one or several FCI channels across a chunk set into `Dataset`s.

    For each requested channel, orders the chunks north -> south by their top-left
    latitude (so the caller may pass them in any order), stitches the radiance
    row-wise, calibrates it to reflectance (solar) or brightness temperature
    (thermal), and returns a geolocated pyramids `Dataset` carrying the
    northernmost chunk's CRS + geotransform. The chunks must share a CRS, cell
    size and column count and be vertically contiguous (validated per channel,
    since channels differ in resolution).

    Pass exactly one of `channel` (returns a `Dataset`) or `channels` (returns a
    `dict[str, Dataset]`); `read_fci(chunks, "ir_105")` is unchanged.

    Args:
        chunks: An ordered iterable of chunks, each either a pyramids `Dataset`
            already holding the channel radiance, or a value accepted by
            `open_chunk` (by default a NetCDF path).
        channel: A single channel identifier (e.g. `"ir_105"`, `"vis_06"`) for a
            `Dataset` result; mutually exclusive with `channels`.
        channels: A sequence of channel identifiers for a `dict[str, Dataset]`
            result; mutually exclusive with `channel`. (Each channel is opened via
            `open_chunk`, whose contract is per-channel; the grid is validated and
            ordered per channel because channels differ in resolution.)
        sensor: Registry sensor name (default `"fci"`).
        calibrate: When `True` (default), calibrate to a physical quantity; when
            `False`, return the stitched raw radiance.
        sun_earth_distance: Sun-earth distance (AU) for solar-channel reflectance.
        cos_sza: Cosine of the solar zenith angle for the reflectance sun-angle
            correction, or `None`.
        coeffs: Per-granule calibration coefficients preferred over the registry
            fallback (see `calibrate_channel`), or `None` to use the registry. They
            override a **single** channel's calibration, so they are only accepted
            with `channel=` — passing `coeffs` together with `channels=[...]` is an
            error (each channel would need its own).
        open_chunk: Callable `(chunk, channel) -> Dataset` used for chunks that
            are not already Datasets. Defaults to a NetCDF reader (see the module
            warning about the FCI layout).

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` (for `channel`) or a `dict[str, Dataset]` keyed by
        channel (for `channels`) of the calibrated (or raw) channel(s) on the
        stitched grid.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When neither / both of `channel` / `channels` are given, or
            when `chunks` is empty.
        CalibrationError: When a channel lacks the constants its kind needs.
        UnknownSensorError: When the sensor / channel is not in the registry.
    """
    requested, single = resolve_channels(channel, channels, "read_fci")
    chunk_list = list(chunks)
    if not chunk_list:
        raise ReaderError("read_fci: no chunks given")
    # A pre-opened Dataset holds exactly one channel's radiance, so it cannot serve
    # a multi-channel request — every channel would alias the same array. Reject it
    # rather than return a physically meaningless dict.
    if not single and any(hasattr(chunk, "read_array") for chunk in chunk_list):
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_fci: channels=[...] needs path-like chunks read per channel via "
            "open_chunk; a pre-opened Dataset already holds a single channel"
        )
    # `coeffs` overrides one channel's calibration; sharing it across a channel set
    # would mis-calibrate the others. Require the single-channel form for an override.
    if not single and coeffs is not None:
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_fci: `coeffs` overrides a single channel's calibration; pass it "
            "with `channel=`, not `channels=[...]` (each channel calibrates on its own)"
        )
    opener = open_chunk or _default_open_chunk

    from pyramids.base.crs import crs_spec
    from pyramids.dataset import Dataset, GeoReference

    results = {}
    for name in requested:
        datasets = [
            chunk if hasattr(chunk, "read_array") else opener(chunk, name)
            for chunk in chunk_list
        ]
        _validate_chunk_grid(datasets)
        # Order the chunks north -> south by their top-left latitude/y so the
        # stitch and geolocation are correct regardless of the order the chunks
        # were passed in (FCI files are commonly numbered south -> north).
        ordered = sorted(datasets, key=lambda ds: ds.geotransform[3], reverse=True)
        radiance = np.concatenate(
            [np.asarray(ds.read_array(), dtype=float) for ds in ordered], axis=0
        )
        data = (
            calibrate_channel(
                radiance, name, sensor, sun_earth_distance, cos_sza, coeffs=coeffs
            )
            if calibrate
            else radiance
        )
        north = ordered[0]
        # Calibration can produce NaN (terminator reflectance / non-positive
        # radiance), so declare NaN as nodata rather than the default -9999.
        results[name] = Dataset.from_array(
            data,
            geo_ref=GeoReference(
                geo=north.geotransform, epsg=crs_spec(north.epsg, north.crs)
            ),
            no_data_value=np.nan,
        )
    return results[requested[0]] if single else results

    pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.seviri #

    MSG-SEVIRI Level-1.5 native (.nat) reader.

    read_seviri decodes one SEVIRI VIS/IR channel from a real MSG Level-1.5 native (.nat) granule and returns a calibrated, geolocated pyramids Dataset (reflectance for a solar channel, brightness temperature for a thermal one).

    The .nat format is a packed binary: an ASCII Main/Secondary Product Header carrying the segment table, a fixed-layout binary 15Header (the Level-1.5 prologue, with the per-granule calibration and the reference grid), then the 15Data image records — one record per scan line, holding a 65-byte side-info header plus 10-bit packed counts for each selected channel in turn (the 11 VIS/IR channels first, then HRV). parse_seviri_native reads the segment table and the 15Header, then for the requested channel unpacks the counts, applies the granule's Cal_Slope / Cal_Offset to get radiance, masks the off-earth (zero-count) corners, and orients the scene north-up / west-left (the grid origin is South-East). read_seviri then calibrates that radiance via the sensor registry.

    Validated against a real Meteosat-10 (MSG3) full-disk granule (see issue #40): IR_108 decodes to brightness temperature in the expected range on the 3 km geostationary grid. HRV (a different, higher-resolution geometry) is out of scope.

    parse_seviri_native(path, channel, *, subsatellite_longitude=0.0) #

    Decode one VIS/IR channel of an MSG Level-1.5 native (.nat) granule.

    Reads the segment table and the fixed-layout 15Header (reference grid, grid step and the per-granule calibration), then unpacks the channel's 10-bit counts from every image line record, applies the granule Cal_Slope / Cal_Offset to get radiance, masks the zero-count (off-earth) corners to NaN, and orients the scene north-up / west-left. Only the image lines actually present are read, so a header-preserved subset (whose header still declares the full disk) decodes correctly rather than reading past end-of-file.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    path Any

    Path to an MSG SEVIRI Level-1.5 native .nat file.

    		 required
    channel str

    A VIS/IR channel identifier (e.g. "IR_108", "VIS006"); HRV is not supported.

    		 required
    subsatellite_longitude float

    Sub-satellite longitude (degrees east) for the geostationary CRS. Defaults to 0.0, the nominal prime service (MSG15); pass the service longitude for IODC (41.5) or rapid-scan (9.5) granules, whose .nat header the reader does not parse for it.

    		 0.0

    def parse_seviri_native(
    path: Any, channel: str, *, subsatellite_longitude: float = 0.0
) -> Any:
    """Decode one VIS/IR channel of an MSG Level-1.5 native (`.nat`) granule.

    Reads the segment table and the fixed-layout ``15Header`` (reference grid,
    grid step and the per-granule calibration), then unpacks the channel's 10-bit
    counts from every image line record, applies the granule ``Cal_Slope`` /
    ``Cal_Offset`` to get radiance, masks the zero-count (off-earth) corners to
    NaN, and orients the scene north-up / west-left. Only the image lines
    actually present are read, so a header-preserved subset (whose header still
    declares the full disk) decodes correctly rather than reading past end-of-file.

    Args:
        path: Path to an MSG SEVIRI Level-1.5 native `.nat` file.
        channel: A VIS/IR channel identifier (e.g. `"IR_108"`, `"VIS006"`); HRV
            is not supported.
        subsatellite_longitude: Sub-satellite longitude (degrees east) for the
            geostationary CRS. Defaults to `0.0`, the nominal prime service
            (`MSG15`); pass the service longitude for IODC (41.5) or rapid-scan
            (9.5) granules, whose `.nat` header the reader does not parse for it.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` holding the channel radiance on the geostationary
        grid, with the geostationary CRS, a metre geotransform, and NaN nodata.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When the channel is unknown / HRV, the file is not a
            recognised MSG Level-1.5 native granule (no segment table, or the
            ``15Header`` layout / calibration fails its sanity checks), the file
            carries no complete line record, or the decoded line records are not
            contiguous (an unexpected channel selection or layout).
    """
    if channel == "HRV":
        raise ReaderError("read_seviri: HRV is not supported (different geometry)")
    try:
        position = _VISIR_CHANNELS.index(channel)
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise ReaderError(
            f"read_seviri: unknown SEVIRI VIS/IR channel {channel!r}"
        ) from exc

    try:
        handle = open(path, "rb")
    except OSError as exc:
        raise ReaderError(f"read_seviri: cannot open {path} ({exc})") from exc
    with handle:
        segments = _segments(handle.read(_PRODUCT_HEADER_SCAN_BYTES))
        try:
            header_length, header_offset = segments["15Header"]
            data_length, data_offset = segments["15Data"]
        except KeyError as exc:
            raise ReaderError(
                "read_seviri: no 15Header/15Data segment table "
                f"(not an MSG Level-1.5 native file?) — {path}"
            ) from exc
        handle.seek(header_offset)
        header = handle.read(header_length)
        if len(header) < _CALIBRATION_OFFSET + 12 * 16:
            raise ReaderError(
                "read_seviri: 15Header is truncated "
                "(not a supported MSG Level-1.5 native file)"
            )
        file_size = os.fstat(handle.fileno()).st_size

    lines_declared, columns = struct.unpack_from(">ii", header, _REF_GRID_OFFSET)
    line_step_km, column_step_km = struct.unpack_from(">ff", header, _GRID_STEP_OFFSET)
    # The reference grid and grid step sit immediately before the calibration
    # block: sane values here confirm the fixed 15Header layout was found. The
    # line and column steps must match (the VIS/IR grid is isotropic 3 km).
    if not (
        lines_declared == columns
        and 1000 <= columns <= 12000
        and 2.9 < column_step_km < 3.1
        and np.isclose(line_step_km, column_step_km)
        and columns % 4 == 0
    ):
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_seviri: unexpected 15Header layout (reference grid / grid step "
            "sanity check failed) — not a supported MSG Level-1.5 native file"
        )
    pixel_m = column_step_km * 1000.0

    slope, offset = struct.unpack_from(
        ">dd", header, _CALIBRATION_OFFSET + position * 16
    )
    if slope <= 0:
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_seviri: non-physical calibration slope (unexpected header layout)"
        )

    if data_length % lines_declared:
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_seviri: 15Data length is not a whole number of line records"
        )
    stride = data_length // lines_declared
    packed_bytes = columns * 10 // 8
    # The 11 VIS/IR channels precede HRV in every record; assume the standard
    # all-channel product so channel `position` maps straight to block `position`.
    # The contiguity check below rejects a file where that assumption does not hold.
    block_start = position * (_LINE_SIDE_INFO_BYTES + packed_bytes)
    data_start = block_start + _LINE_SIDE_INFO_BYTES
    if data_start + packed_bytes > stride:
        raise ReaderError("read_seviri: channel block exceeds the line-record stride")

    # The declared 15Data holds exactly `lines_declared` records; a full product
    # has a 15Trailer segment after it, so cap the count at the declared line
    # count. Without this cap the trailer bytes get read as extra "line records",
    # break the +1 contiguity of `line_numbers`, and reject a valid full disk.
    # The file-size term still handles a header-preserved subset (fewer records).
    available = min((file_size - data_offset) // stride, lines_declared)
    if available < 1:
        raise ReaderError("read_seviri: file carries no complete image line record")

    counts = np.empty((available, columns), dtype=np.uint16)
    line_numbers = np.empty(available, dtype=np.int64)
    with (
        open(path, "rb") as handle,
        mmap.mmap(handle.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ) as mapped,
    ):
        for index in range(available):
            record = data_offset + index * stride
            line_numbers[index] = struct.unpack_from(
                ">i", mapped, record + block_start + _LINE_NUMBER_OFFSET
            )[0]
            start = record + data_start
            counts[index] = _unpack_10bit(mapped[start : start + packed_bytes], columns)

    if not np.all(np.diff(line_numbers) == 1):
        raise ReaderError(
            "read_seviri: image line records are not contiguous "
            "(unexpected channel selection or record layout)"
        )

    radiance = counts.astype(float) * slope + offset
    radiance[counts == 0] = np.nan  # zero counts mark the off-earth space corners
    # The grid origin is South-East: line numbers increase northward and the
    # stored columns run east -> west (the first column is East). Reverse both
    # axes for a north-up, west-left raster. Copy the flipped view to a
    # C-contiguous array so no downstream consumer trips on the negative strides.
    radiance = np.ascontiguousarray(radiance[::-1, ::-1])

    # CGMS/EUMETSAT navigation places the sub-satellite point at the CENTRE of the
    # reference pixel N/2 (0-based, both axes; e.g. pixel 1856 of the 3712 grid) —
    # the COFF = LOFF convention, which reproduces the published MSG full-disk area
    # extent (west edge -(N/2 + 0.5) * px). All columns are present (full width) so
    # the SSP column is N/2; only a subset of lines may be present, so the SSP row
    # is N/2 measured from the northmost present line (row 0 after the north-up
    # flip). Register the metre geotransform so that reference pixel's centre is
    # (x=0, y=0).
    reference = columns / 2.0  # == lines_declared / 2.0 for the square VIS/IR grid
    ssp_row = int(line_numbers[-1]) - reference
    x_west_edge = -(reference + 0.5) * pixel_m
    y_north_edge = (ssp_row + 0.5) * pixel_m
    geo = (x_west_edge, pixel_m, 0.0, y_north_edge, 0.0, -pixel_m)

    from pyramids.dataset import Dataset, GeoReference

    dataset = Dataset.from_array(
        radiance, geo_ref=GeoReference(geo=geo, epsg=None), no_data_value=np.nan
    )
    dataset.crs = _geostationary_wkt(subsatellite_longitude)
    return dataset

    def read_seviri(
    source: Any,
    channel: str,
    *,
    sensor: str = "seviri",
    calibrate: bool = True,
    sun_earth_distance: float = 1.0,
    cos_sza: Any = None,
    coeffs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    parse: Any = None,
    subsatellite_longitude: float = 0.0,
) -> Any:
    """Read one SEVIRI channel into a calibrated, geolocated `Dataset`.

    Decodes the channel radiance (from a `.nat` granule via `parse`, or straight
    from a `Dataset` source), then calibrates it to reflectance (solar) or
    brightness temperature (thermal) via the registry and returns a pyramids
    `Dataset` carrying the source's CRS + geotransform.

    Args:
        source: A path to an MSG Level-1.5 native `.nat` file (decoded by
            `parse`), or a pyramids `Dataset` already holding the channel radiance.
        channel: Channel identifier (e.g. `"IR_108"`, `"VIS006"`).
        sensor: Registry sensor name (default `"seviri"`).
        calibrate: When `True` (default), calibrate to a physical quantity; when
            `False`, return the raw radiance.
        sun_earth_distance: Sun-earth distance (AU) for solar-channel reflectance.
            The default `1.0` leaves reflectance up to ~3.4% off (`d` ranges
            ~0.983-1.017 AU over the year); pass the granule's `d` for absolute
            accuracy.
        cos_sza: Cosine of the solar zenith angle for the reflectance sun-angle
            correction, or `None`.
        coeffs: Per-granule calibration coefficients preferred over the registry
            fallback (see `calibrate_channel`), or `None` to use the registry.
        parse: Callable `(source, channel) -> Dataset` used when `source` is not
            already a `Dataset`. Defaults to the native `.nat` parser
            (`parse_seviri_native`).
        subsatellite_longitude: Sub-satellite longitude (degrees east) passed to
            the default native parser for the geostationary CRS (default `0.0`,
            the prime service); ignored when a custom `parse` is supplied.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` of the calibrated (or raw) channel.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When `source` is `None`, or the native parse fails.
        CalibrationError: When a channel lacks the constants its kind needs.
        UnknownSensorError: When the sensor / channel is not in the registry.
    """
    if source is None:
        raise ReaderError("read_seviri: source is required")

    if hasattr(source, "read_array"):
        dataset = source
    elif parse is not None:
        dataset = parse(source, channel)
    else:
        dataset = parse_seviri_native(
            source, channel, subsatellite_longitude=subsatellite_longitude
        )
    radiance = np.asarray(dataset.read_array(), dtype=float)
    data = (
        calibrate_channel(
            radiance, channel, sensor, sun_earth_distance, cos_sza, coeffs=coeffs
        )
        if calibrate
        else radiance
    )

    from pyramids.dataset import Dataset, GeoReference

    # Calibration can produce NaN (terminator reflectance / non-positive
    # radiance), so declare NaN as nodata rather than the default -9999.
    epsg = dataset.epsg if dataset.epsg else None
    result = Dataset.from_array(
        data,
        geo_ref=GeoReference(geo=dataset.geotransform, epsg=epsg),
        no_data_value=np.nan,
    )
    if epsg is None:
        # A non-EPSG CRS (e.g. the geostationary grid) must be carried explicitly.
        result.crs = dataset.crs
    return result

    pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci #

    Sentinel-3 OLCI Level-1B (EFR / ERR) reader -- native, satpy-free.

    read_olci(granule, channel="Oa08") decodes one OLCI radiance band (or several via channels=[...]) out of a .SEN3 granule into a pyramids Dataset, through pyramids' bundled GDAL NetCDF driver. No netCDF4, and nothing from the satpy stack.

    OLCI is a pushbroom swath instrument, so the result carries its geolocation as a GDAL GEOLOCATION domain pointing at the granule's per-pixel geo_coordinates.nc longitude / latitude arrays -- not an affine geotransform, which cannot describe a swath. The reader resamples nothing; a caller who wants a map grid warps the result themselves (gdal.Warp(..., geoloc=True)).

    Per issue #136 this decodes to arrays plus standard CF metadata only: radiometric calibration choices (radiance -> reflectance) stay with the callers and the composites tier, and the granule's own instrument_data.nc carries the solar_flux needed for that conversion.

    def available_olci_channels(source: Any) -> list[str]:
    """List the OLCI radiance bands a granule actually carries.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or a file inside it.

    Returns:
        The canonical channel names present, sorted (`["Oa01", "Oa02", ...]`).

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When `source` is not a granule directory or a file in one.
    """
    granule = resolve_granule(source, "available_olci_channels")
    found = []
    for number in range(1, _BAND_COUNT + 1):
        channel = f"Oa{number:02d}"
        if (granule / _band_filename(channel)).is_file():
            found.append(channel)
    return found

    product_type(granule) #

    Detect whether a granule is the full- or reduced-resolution OLCI product.

    EFR and ERR granules hold the same OaNN_radiance.nc filenames and the same variable names, so the product type -- and therefore the ground resolution, 300 m against ~1200 m -- is only knowable from the granule's own naming or its manifest. Both are checked -- the name first, then xfdumanifest.xml -- and None means neither identified the product, in which case the reader reports no resolution rather than asserting a wrong one.

    An ambiguous source is treated exactly like a silent one: a text carrying both tokens yields None rather than the first match, because an ERR granule routinely references the EFR product it was derived from, so preferring either one would be a guess (see _product_tokens).

      >>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
>>> product_type(Path("S3A_OL_1_EFR____20230101T101530.SEN3"))
'EFR'
>>> product_type(Path("S3B_OL_1_ERR____20230101T101530.SEN3"))
'ERR'
    • A granule that names neither, and carries no manifest saying so, yields None -- which is what makes the reader omit resolution_m rather than guess it:

>>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
>>> product_type(Path("mystery.SEN3")) is None
True
    • A name claiming both products is ambiguous, so it too yields None rather than the first token found:

>>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
>>> product_type(Path("S3A_OL_1_ERR____from_OL_1_EFR_source.SEN3")) is None
True

    def product_type(granule: Path) -> str | None:
    """Detect whether a granule is the full- or reduced-resolution OLCI product.

    EFR and ERR granules hold the **same** `OaNN_radiance.nc` filenames and the
    same variable names, so the product type -- and therefore the ground
    resolution, 300 m against ~1200 m -- is only knowable from the granule's own
    naming or its manifest. Both are checked -- the name first, then
    `xfdumanifest.xml` -- and `None` means neither identified the product, in
    which case the reader reports no resolution rather than asserting a wrong one.

    An **ambiguous** source is treated exactly like a silent one: a text carrying
    both tokens yields `None` rather than the first match, because an ERR granule
    routinely references the EFR product it was derived from, so preferring either
    one would be a guess (see `_product_tokens`).

    Args:
        granule: The `.SEN3` granule directory.

    Returns:
        `"EFR"`, `"ERR"`, or `None` -- when the granule does not identify itself,
        and equally when it names both products.

    Examples:
        - A standard product name identifies itself, so no file access is needed:
            ```python
            >>> from pathlib import Path
            >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
            >>> product_type(Path("S3A_OL_1_EFR____20230101T101530.SEN3"))
            'EFR'
            >>> product_type(Path("S3B_OL_1_ERR____20230101T101530.SEN3"))
            'ERR'

            ```
        - A granule that names neither, and carries no manifest saying so, yields
          `None` -- which is what makes the reader omit `resolution_m` rather than
          guess it:
            ```python
            >>> from pathlib import Path
            >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
            >>> product_type(Path("mystery.SEN3")) is None
            True

            ```
        - A name claiming both products is ambiguous, so it too yields `None`
          rather than the first token found:
            ```python
            >>> from pathlib import Path
            >>> from pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.olci import product_type
            >>> product_type(Path("S3A_OL_1_ERR____from_OL_1_EFR_source.SEN3")) is None
            True

            ```
    """
    found = _product_tokens(granule.name.upper(), "_OL_1_")
    if found is not None:
        return found
    manifest = granule / "xfdumanifest.xml"
    if manifest.is_file():
        try:
            text = manifest.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").upper()
        except OSError:
            return None
        return _product_tokens(text, "OL_1_")
    return None

    def read_olci_band(source: Any, channel: Any, *, geolocation: bool = True) -> Any:
    """Decode a single OLCI radiance band from a `.SEN3` granule.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or a file inside it.
        channel: The band to read (`"Oa08"`, `"oa8"`, `"Oa08_radiance"`).
        geolocation: When `True` (default), attach the granule's per-pixel
            `GEOLOCATION` domain. `False` returns the array on its placeholder
            pixel grid only -- useful when the geolocation file is absent or the
            caller only wants the counts.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` of the unpacked radiance, NaN where the granule
        flags a fill / out-of-range pixel, with CF metadata and (by default) the
        swath `GEOLOCATION` domain.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When the channel name is not an OLCI band, the granule has
            no such band file, or the variable cannot be decoded. With
            `geolocation=True` it also raises when `geo_coordinates.nc` or its
            longitude / latitude variables are missing, when that grid's shape
            does not match the band (an oversized annotation grid would otherwise
            place every pixel wrongly, silently), or when its `scale_factor` /
            `add_offset` is non-finite or the scale is zero.

    Note:
        A `_FillValue` that is not a finite number cannot mask anything, so the
        decode emits a `UserWarning` and the result's nodata is incomplete rather
        than the read failing (see `invalid_mask`).
    """
    reader = "read_olci"
    name = _canonical_channel(channel, reader)
    granule = resolve_granule(source, reader)
    # Decode first: the geolocation grid is validated against the band's shape, so
    # the shape has to be known before the domain can be built.
    data, variable_meta = _read_band(granule, name, reader)
    domain = _resolve_domain(granule, reader, data.shape) if geolocation else {}
    return _wrap_band(granule, name, data, variable_meta, domain, product_type(granule))

    def read_olci(
    source: Any,
    channel: str | None = None,
    *,
    channels: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    geolocation: bool = True,
) -> Any:
    """Read one or several OLCI L1B radiance bands from a `.SEN3` granule.

    Decodes each requested band's packed `OaNN_radiance` variable (`raw *
    scale_factor + add_offset`, with the `_FillValue` and anything outside the
    variable's validity limits masked to NaN) and returns it as a swath `Dataset`
    carrying the granule's per-pixel geolocation as a GDAL `GEOLOCATION` domain.
    The limits come from the `valid_min` / `valid_max` scalars the OLCI L1
    specification carries -- not from a combined `valid_range`, which appears
    nowhere in it -- and are compared against the raw, still-packed values.

    Pass exactly one of `channel` (returns a `Dataset`) or `channels` (returns a
    `dict[str, Dataset]` keyed by canonical channel name).

    This reader **decodes only** -- it does not convert radiance to reflectance
    (issue #136 scopes radiometric calibration choices out). The granule's
    `instrument_data.nc` carries the per-detector `solar_flux` a caller needs for
    that conversion.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or any file inside it.
        channel: A single band (`"Oa08"`); mutually exclusive with `channels`.
        channels: A sequence of bands for a `dict` result; mutually exclusive
            with `channel`.
        geolocation: When `True` (default), attach each result's per-pixel
            `GEOLOCATION` domain from `geo_coordinates.nc`.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` (for `channel`) or a `dict[str, Dataset]` (for
        `channels`), each on the granule's native swath grid with NaN nodata.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When neither / both of `channel` / `channels` are given,
            `channels` is empty or has duplicates, a band name is not an OLCI
            band, or the granule lacks a requested band. A channel set whose bands
            come back on **different** shapes also raises: the one geolocation
            domain is shared across the set, which is only sound because the bands
            of a granule share a grid, so a granule that breaks that is reported
            rather than geolocated against the wrong grid. With
            `geolocation=True`, also when `geo_coordinates.nc` or its variables are
            missing, its grid's shape differs from the bands', or it carries an
            unusable `scale_factor` / `add_offset`.

    Note:
        A `_FillValue` that is not a finite number cannot mask anything, so the
        decode emits a `UserWarning` per affected band and the result's nodata is
        incomplete rather than the read failing (see `invalid_mask`).
    """
    requested, single = resolve_channels(channel, channels, "read_olci")
    # Canonicalise before the duplicate check: `resolve_channels` compares the raw
    # strings, so aliases of one band ("Oa08" and "oa8") slip through it and would
    # otherwise collapse into a single dict entry, silently dropping a requested band.
    canonical = [_canonical_channel(name, "read_olci") for name in requested]
    if len(set(canonical)) != len(canonical):
        duplicates = sorted({c for c in canonical if canonical.count(c) > 1})
        raise ReaderError(
            f"read_olci: `channels` names the same band more than once (after "
            f"normalising spellings): {duplicates}"
        )
    # Resolve the granule and its geolocation domain ONCE for the whole set,
    # matching read_fci_l1c's documented read-each-chunk-once pattern rather than
    # re-running them per channel.
    reader = "read_olci"
    granule = resolve_granule(source, reader)
    # Detect the product type once for the whole set rather than per band: it may
    # read xfdumanifest.xml, which a 21-band read would otherwise re-parse 21 times.
    product = product_type(granule)
    decoded = {name: _read_band(granule, name, reader) for name in canonical}
    shapes = {name: values.shape for name, (values, _) in decoded.items()}
    if len(set(shapes.values())) > 1:
        raise ReaderError(
            f"read_olci: the requested bands are not on one grid: {shapes}; OLCI "
            f"bands of a granule share a grid, so this granule looks inconsistent"
        )
    first = next(iter(decoded.values()))[0]
    domain = _resolve_domain(granule, reader, first.shape) if geolocation else {}
    results = {
        name: _wrap_band(granule, name, values, variable_meta, domain, product)
        for name, (values, variable_meta) in decoded.items()
    }
    return results[canonical[0]] if single else results

    pyramids_eo.sensors.readers.slstr #

    Sentinel-3 SLSTR Level-1 RBT reader -- native, satpy-free.

    read_slstr(granule, channel="S5") decodes one SLSTR channel (or several via channels=[...]) out of a .SEN3 granule into a pyramids Dataset, through pyramids' bundled GDAL NetCDF driver. No netCDF4, and nothing from the satpy stack.

    SLSTR is dual-view and multi-grid, which drives this reader's two extra arguments:

    • view -- the instrument images each scene twice, "nadir" (straight down) and "oblique" (slanted, ~55 deg forward). Each view is a separate grid.
    • grid -- channels live on different resolutions: the solar channels S1-S6 on the 500 m a grid (with S4-S6 duplicated onto the alternative 500 m b), the thermal S7-S9 on the 1 km i grid, and of the fire channels F1 on the 1 km f grid but F2 on i -- they are asymmetric, and there is no F2_BT_f*.nc. read_slstr tries each channel's documented grids in order (F1 falls back to i for products predating the f baseline), and grid= restricts the read to one grid. available_slstr_channels reports what a particular granule actually carries.

    Because the grids differ in shape, a multi-channel read returns a dict rather than a stack -- channels=["S5", "S8"] yields arrays of different sizes.

    Like OLCI, SLSTR is a swath instrument, so a result carries its geolocation as a GDAL GEOLOCATION domain over the matching geodetic_* annotation file rather than an affine geotransform, and this reader resamples nothing.

    Per issue #136 this decodes to arrays plus standard CF metadata only. Note the RBT product is already geophysical: S1-S6 are radiances and S7-S9 / F1-F2 are brightness temperatures in kelvin as shipped, so no Planck conversion is applied (or needed) here.

    def available_slstr_channels(
    source: Any, *, view: str = "nadir"
) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    """Report which channels a granule carries in one view, and on which grids.

    This is how a caller discovers a product's real layout rather than assuming
    it -- including that `F2` lives on the 1 km `i` grid while `F1` is on `f`, and
    which of `S4`-`S6` are duplicated onto the alternative 500 m `b` grid.

    A grid is listed only when the granule holds **both** the measurement file and
    the `geodetic_<grid><view>.nc` the measurement needs, so what this reports is
    what `read_slstr` can actually return -- a measurement whose annotation file is
    missing would raise there, and listing it would promise a read that fails. A
    granule stripped of its geodetic files therefore reports `{}` even though the
    measurement files are all present.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or a file inside it.
        view: `"nadir"` (default) or `"oblique"`.

    Returns:
        A `{channel: [grid letters]}` mapping listing only the channels the granule
        holds a measurement **and** a matching geodetic file for, in the product's
        own channel order -- `S1`..`S9` then `F1`, `F2` -- which is not the
        alphabetical order the error messages use. Each channel's grid letters are
        likewise in the order `read_slstr` would try them.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When `source` is not a granule, or `view` is not an SLSTR
            view.
    """
    reader = "available_slstr_channels"
    suffix = _resolve_view(view, reader)
    granule = resolve_granule(source, reader)
    found: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
    for channel, (grids, quantity) in _CHANNEL_GRIDS.items():
        present = [
            letter
            for letter in grids
            if (granule / f"{channel}_{quantity}_{letter}{suffix}.nc").is_file()
            and (granule / f"geodetic_{letter}{suffix}.nc").is_file()
        ]
        if present:
            found[channel] = present
    return found

    def read_slstr_band(
    source: Any,
    channel: Any,
    *,
    view: str | None = None,
    grid: str | None = None,
    geolocation: bool = True,
) -> Any:
    """Decode a single SLSTR channel from a `.SEN3` granule.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or a file inside it.
        channel: The channel to read (`"S5"`, `"s5"`, `"F1"`), or the product's
            own variable spelling (`"S5_radiance_bn"`), whose grid and view then
            select the file -- passing a conflicting `grid=` / `view=` is an error
            rather than one of the two being silently ignored.
        view: `"nadir"` or `"oblique"`. `None` (default) takes the view from a
            spelled channel, falling back to nadir.
        grid: An explicit grid letter (`"a"`, `"b"`, `"i"`, `"f"`) restricting the
            read to that one grid. `None` (default) tries the channel's documented
            grids in order. The restriction is honoured even when only one
            candidate file exists, so a read never silently returns a different
            resolution than the one asked for.
        geolocation: When `True` (default), attach the `GEOLOCATION` domain from
            the `geodetic_*` file matching the grid read.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` of the channel -- radiance for `S1`-`S6`, brightness
        temperature in kelvin for `S7`-`S9` / `F1`-`F2` -- NaN where the granule
        flags a fill / out-of-range pixel, with CF metadata and (by default) the
        swath `GEOLOCATION` domain.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When the channel, view or `grid` is not an SLSTR one, when a
            spelled channel names a quantity that channel does not ship
            (`"S9_radiance_an"`), when a spelled channel's grid / view contradicts
            an explicit `grid=` / `view=`, or when the granule has no measurement
            for that channel, view and grid. With `geolocation=True` it also raises
            when the matching geodetic file or its longitude / latitude variables
            are missing, when that annotation grid's shape does not match the band
            (an oversized one would otherwise place every pixel wrongly, silently),
            or when its `scale_factor` / `add_offset` is non-finite or the scale is
            zero.

    Note:
        A `_FillValue` that is not a finite number cannot mask anything, so the
        decode emits a `UserWarning` and the result's nodata is incomplete rather
        than the read failing (see `invalid_mask`).
    """
    reader = "read_slstr"
    name, letter, suffix = _resolve_channel_target(channel, view, grid, reader)
    granule = resolve_granule(source, reader)
    band_path, found_grid = _discover_band_file(granule, name, suffix, reader, letter)

    data, variable_meta = read_packed_variable(band_path, band_path.stem, reader=reader)
    domain = (
        _geodetic_domain(granule, found_grid, suffix, reader, data.shape)
        if geolocation
        else {}
    )
    dataset = wrap_swath(data, domain)
    dataset.band_names = [name]
    dataset.raster.SetMetadata(
        _channel_metadata(
            name,
            granule,
            found_grid,
            suffix,
            variable_meta,
            geolocated=bool(domain),
        )
    )
    return dataset

    read_slstr(source, channel=None, *, channels=None, view=None, grid=None, geolocation=True) #

    Read one or several SLSTR L1 RBT channels from a .SEN3 granule.

    Decodes each requested channel's packed variable (raw * scale_factor + add_offset, with the _FillValue and anything outside the variable's validity limits masked to NaN) and returns it as a swath Dataset carrying the matching grid's per-pixel geolocation as a GDAL GEOLOCATION domain. The limits come from the valid_min / valid_max scalars the SLSTR L1 specification carries -- not from a combined valid_range, which appears nowhere in it -- and are compared against the raw, still-packed values.

    Pass exactly one of channel (returns a Dataset) or channels (returns a dict[str, Dataset]). Channels on different grids have different array shapes, which is why a channel set returns a dict rather than a stack.

    Either may also be given in the product's own variable spelling ("S5_radiance_bn"), and the grid and view it carries then select the file: they are honoured, not merely tolerated. So a channel set may mix views and grids per channel -- channels=["S5_radiance_an", "S8_BT_io"] reads one nadir and one oblique -- while view= / grid= supply whatever a bare spelling leaves open. A spelling that contradicts an explicit view= / grid= is an error rather than one of the two being silently ignored.

    def read_slstr(
    source: Any,
    channel: str | None = None,
    *,
    channels: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    view: str | None = None,
    grid: str | None = None,
    geolocation: bool = True,
) -> Any:
    """Read one or several SLSTR L1 RBT channels from a `.SEN3` granule.

    Decodes each requested channel's packed variable (`raw * scale_factor +
    add_offset`, with the `_FillValue` and anything outside the variable's
    validity limits masked to NaN) and returns it as a swath `Dataset` carrying
    the matching grid's per-pixel geolocation as a GDAL `GEOLOCATION` domain. The
    limits come from the `valid_min` / `valid_max` scalars the SLSTR L1
    specification carries -- not from a combined `valid_range`, which appears
    nowhere in it -- and are compared against the raw, still-packed values.

    Pass exactly one of `channel` (returns a `Dataset`) or `channels` (returns a
    `dict[str, Dataset]`). Channels on different grids have **different array
    shapes**, which is why a channel set returns a dict rather than a stack.

    Either may also be given in the product's own variable spelling
    (`"S5_radiance_bn"`), and the grid and view it carries then **select the
    file**: they are honoured, not merely tolerated. So a channel set may mix views
    and grids per channel -- `channels=["S5_radiance_an", "S8_BT_io"]` reads one
    nadir and one oblique -- while `view=` / `grid=` supply whatever a bare
    spelling leaves open. A spelling that contradicts an explicit `view=` / `grid=`
    is an error rather than one of the two being silently ignored.

    This reader **decodes only** -- issue #136 scopes radiometric calibration
    choices out. The RBT product is already geophysical, so `S7`-`S9` / `F1`-`F2`
    arrive as brightness temperature in kelvin with no conversion applied.

    Args:
        source: The `.SEN3` granule directory, or any file inside it.
        channel: A single channel (`"S5"`, or `"S5_radiance_bn"`); mutually
            exclusive with `channels`.
        channels: A sequence of channels for a `dict` result; mutually exclusive
            with `channel`. The dict is keyed by **canonical** channel name, so two
            spellings of one channel -- even on different grids, as
            `["S5_radiance_an", "S5_radiance_bn"]` -- are rejected as a duplicate
            rather than collapsing into one entry.
        view: `"nadir"` or `"oblique"` -- SLSTR images each scene twice. `None`
            (default) takes each channel's view from its own spelling, falling back
            to nadir for a bare one.
        grid: An explicit grid letter (`"a"`, `"b"`, `"i"`, `"f"`) restricting
            every channel to that one grid. `None` (default) uses a spelled grid
            where one is given and otherwise tries the channel's documented grids
            in order. A restricted read never falls back to another resolution: a
            channel the granule does not carry on that grid raises instead.
        geolocation: When `True` (default), attach each result's `GEOLOCATION`
            domain.

    Returns:
        A pyramids `Dataset` (for `channel`) or a `dict[str, Dataset]` (for
        `channels`), each on its native swath grid with NaN nodata.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When neither / both of `channel` / `channels` are given,
            `channels` is empty or names a channel twice, a channel or the view
            is not an SLSTR one, a spelled channel names a quantity that channel
            does not ship or a grid / view contradicting an explicit `grid=` /
            `view=`, `grid` is not one of the four SLSTR grid letters, or the
            granule lacks a requested channel on the grid(s) tried. With
            `geolocation=True`, also when a channel's geodetic annotation is
            missing, is on a grid whose shape differs from the band, or carries an
            unusable `scale_factor` / `add_offset`.

    Note:
        A `_FillValue` that is not a finite number cannot mask anything, so the
        decode emits a `UserWarning` per affected channel and the result's nodata
        is incomplete rather than the read failing (see `invalid_mask`).
    """
    requested, single = resolve_channels(channel, channels, "read_slstr")
    # Canonicalise before the duplicate check: `resolve_channels` compares the raw
    # strings, so aliases of one channel ("S5" and "s5") slip through it and would
    # otherwise collapse into a single dict entry, silently dropping a request.
    canonical = [_canonical_channel(name, "read_slstr") for name in requested]
    if len(set(canonical)) != len(canonical):
        duplicates = sorted({c for c in canonical if canonical.count(c) > 1})
        raise ReaderError(
            f"read_slstr: `channels` names the same channel more than once (after "
            f"normalising spellings): {duplicates}"
        )
    # Pass the caller's ORIGINAL spelling through, not the canonical name: a
    # spelled grid and view select a specific file, and canonicalising first would
    # strip them and read a different one.
    # Resolve the granule once for the whole set rather than per channel, matching
    # read_fci_l1c's and read_olci's read-once pattern.
    granule = resolve_granule(source, "read_slstr")
    results = {
        name: read_slstr_band(
            granule, spelling, view=view, grid=grid, geolocation=geolocation
        )
        for name, spelling in zip(canonical, requested)
    }
    return results[canonical[0]] if single else results

    def harmonise(bands: Any, reference: Any, *, method: str | None = None) -> Any:
    """Align a set of bands onto a reference grid.

    Args:
        bands: The bands to harmonise — a mapping `{name: Dataset}` or an
            iterable of pyramids `Dataset`s. Each is resampled onto `reference`'s
            grid (CRS + rows/columns + cell size).
        reference: A pyramids `Dataset` whose grid every band is aligned to.
        method: Resampling method. `None` (default) / `"nearest"` uses
            `Dataset.align` (nearest-neighbour onto the exact reference grid); any
            other value (e.g. `"bilinear"`, `"cubic"`) uses `warped_view` onto the
            reference's CRS + cell size + bbox — preferable for continuous
            reflectance / brightness-temperature bands.

    Returns:
        The aligned bands in the same container shape as the input: a `dict`
        `{name: Dataset}` for a mapping, else a `list[Dataset]`.

    Raises:
        ReaderError: When `reference` is `None`, or when `bands` is empty.
    """
    if reference is None:
        raise ReaderError("harmonise: a reference grid is required")

    if isinstance(bands, dict):
        if not bands:
            raise ReaderError("harmonise: no bands given")
        return {
            name: _resample_to(band, reference, method) for name, band in bands.items()
        }

    band_list = list(bands)
    if not band_list:
        raise ReaderError("harmonise: no bands given")
    return [_resample_to(band, reference, method) for band in band_list]

    Raster-driver plugins#

    The EO readers are also registered as pyramids.raster_drivers plugins (the hook pyramids-core 0.70 added), so pyramids.dataset.Dataset.read_file(<source>) can route a source straight into pyramids-eo — no import of this package needed at the call site. Installing pyramids-eo is the whole integration. The Reading EO sources via read_file guide covers the dispatch rules, the open_options contract, and per-source recipes in full; the essentials:

    driver name source reader
    earthengine ee://<asset-id> from_earthengine
    seviri a .nat granule read_seviri
    ahi an HSD granule named HS_….DAT (optionally .bz2) read_ahi
    s2 a .SAFE product (or .SAFE.zip) from_sentinel2
    fci an FCI L1C granule: a chunk directory, a glob, or an fci:// path read_fci_l1c
    olci a Sentinel-3 OLCI .SEN3 granule directory, or an olci:// path read_olci
    slstr a Sentinel-3 SLSTR .SEN3 granule directory, or a slstr:// path read_slstr 
    from pyramids.dataset import Dataset

# auto-routed: GDAL cannot open these, so read_file falls through to the plugin
nat = Dataset.read_file("MSG_SEVIRI.nat", open_options={"channel": "IR_108"})
ee = Dataset.read_file("ee://USGS/SRTMGL1_003", open_options={"bbox": (0, 0, 1, 1)})
fci = Dataset.read_file("/data/fci_granule", open_options={"channel": "ir_105"})
fci2 = Dataset.read_file("fci:///data/fci_granule", open_options={"channel": "ir_105"})

# Himawari AHI: claimed by the HSD file-name convention, not by the generic .dat suffix,
# and the granule names its own band so open_options may be omitted entirely
ahi = Dataset.read_file("HS_H08_20150415_0230_B13_FLDK_R20_S0101.DAT")

# Sentinel-3: OLCI and SLSTR share the .SEN3 suffix, so the granule's contents decide
# which driver claims it (an olci:// / slstr:// prefix, or driver=, names one explicitly)
olci = Dataset.read_file("S3A_OL_1_EFR.SEN3", open_options={"channel": "Oa08"})
slstr = Dataset.read_file(
    "S3A_SL_1_RBT.SEN3", open_options={"channel": "S8", "view": "oblique"}
)

# Sentinel-2: a product directory auto-routes (GDAL cannot open one), and a zipped
# product auto-routes too because the driver pre-empts GDAL for `.zip`
s2 = Dataset.read_file("S2A_MSIL2A.SAFE", open_options={"bands": ["B04", "B03", "B02"]})
s2z = Dataset.read_file("S2A_MSIL2A.SAFE.zip", open_options={"bands": ["B04"]})

    read_file forwards only open_options to a driver, so reader keywords (channel, bbox, bands, credentials, …) are passed there; options needing a non-string type (e.g. S2 resolution=10) must be given in dict form, not a KEY=VALUE list. A bare read_file("…SAFE") on a product directory reads the product: GDAL cannot open one, so the driver claims it on the fallback. A zipped product reads bare too: the driver declares preempts = (".zip",), so it is tried before GDAL would return a container. Narrow a zipped read with bands / resolution — a whole product is ~10 GiB. Which driver claims a .SAFE is decided by its contents, not its name: ESA shares the suffix with Sentinel-1, and those products stay with GDAL.

    pyramids_eo.drivers #

    Raster-reader drivers for the pyramids.raster_drivers plugin hook.

    pyramids-core 0.70 added a pyramids.raster_drivers entry-point group: a third-party package registers a driver class there, and Dataset.read_file(<source>) routes a source GDAL cannot open into that driver with no import coupling. This subpackage registers pyramids-eo's readers:

    • :class:~pyramids_eo.drivers.earthengine.EarthEngineDriver — ee://<asset-id> sources.
    • :class:~pyramids_eo.drivers.seviri.SeviriDriver — SEVIRI native .nat granules.
    • :class:~pyramids_eo.drivers.ahi.AhiDriver — Himawari AHI Himawari Standard Data (.DAT) granules. It is one of two drivers here that declare a suffix and then deliberately narrow it in can_open — Sentinel-2 is the other, inspecting a product's contents to tell the mission apart: .dat is too generic, so it matches the HSD file-name convention instead (see its docstring).
    • :class:~pyramids_eo.drivers.sentinel2.Sentinel2Driver — Sentinel-2 .SAFE products.
    • :class:~pyramids_eo.drivers.fci.FciDriver — MTG-FCI L1C FDHSI granules (a chunk set named by a directory or glob).
    • :class:~pyramids_eo.drivers.olci.OlciDriver — Sentinel-3 OLCI L1B .SEN3 granules.
    • :class:~pyramids_eo.drivers.slstr.SlstrDriver — Sentinel-3 SLSTR L1 RBT .SEN3 granules.

    OLCI and SLSTR products share the .SEN3 directory suffix, so both drivers claim it and their can_open predicates disambiguate on content — an OLCI granule holds Oa*_radiance.nc band files, an SLSTR one holds S*_radiance_*.nc / *_BT_*.nc. An olci:// or slstr:// prefix (or driver=) names one explicitly. Deciding on content has two consequences worth stating, since neither is obvious from the claim set:

    • A .SEN3 holding both kinds of file is claimed by both drivers, and select_driver takes the first claimant in registration order, which is alphabetical — so olci wins. The outcome is stable rather than arbitrary, and a scheme prefix or driver= overrides it.
    • An empty or incomplete .SEN3 is claimed by neither, so read_file surfaces GDAL's own "not recognized" error instead of the readers' more useful "the product looks incomplete or is not the expected Sentinel-3 level/type". Calling read_olci / read_slstr directly, or passing driver=, reaches that better message.

    A boolean reader keyword passed through read_file arrives as a string, because Dataset.read_file normalises open_options to GDAL's KEY=VALUE form. The drivers translate those spellings (see :func:~pyramids_eo.drivers._base.coerce_booleans) rather than letting the truthy string "false" switch an option on.

    The entry points in pyproject.toml are the whole integration; installing the package is enough for read_file to find these. Each driver is a thin wrapper over an existing reader (from_earthengine / read_seviri / read_ahi / from_sentinel2 / read_fci_l1c / read_olci / read_slstr), which stays the ergonomic public API.

    Only a driver's read is reachable this way: Dataset.read_file never dispatches read_collection, so :meth:~pyramids_eo.drivers.earthengine.EarthEngineDriver.read_collection is declared and implemented but unreachable through the facade — a temporal stack goes through collection_from_earthengine.

    A single read_file source string can name a set of files — a directory, a glob, or an fci:// path — which is how a multi-chunk FCI granule is addressed (see :func:~pyramids_eo.drivers._base.expand_sources). Sentinel-2 reaches this layer on the bare path in both its forms: a product directory through the post-GDAL can_open fallback (GDAL cannot open one), and a zipped product through pre-emption — :class:~pyramids_eo.drivers.sentinel2. Sentinel2Driver declares preempts = (".zip",), the opt-in pyramids-core 0.71 added (serapeum-org/pyramids-core#1344), because GDAL would otherwise open the archive and return a bare container. Because ESA shares .SAFE across missions, can_open identifies the mission from the product's contents rather than its name, so a Sentinel-1 product — zipped or not — is left to GDAL instead of failing in the Sentinel-2 reader.
